Do not read across the two too literally: this toy is small enough that the right baseline removes all the variance, which is the best case, whereas the figure shows the more typical outcome of a large reduction rather than a total one. And note what happened in case 4: the baseline extracted a useful update from a failure, which the naive estimator threw away.

Words you will hear
Score function — \(\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\); also "log-derivative trick", "likelihood-ratio estimator". Vanilla policy gradient (VPG) — REINFORCE plus a learned value baseline; the thing PPO improves on. Control variate — the statistics name for a baseline: a zero-mean term subtracted to cut variance. Unbiased — correct on average over infinite samples, which says nothing about how noisy any one sample is. Credit assignment — deciding which of many actions caused an outcome. On-policy — the update is only valid for data generated by the current policy; off-policy methods reuse older data (Chapter 4).

2.5 Actor-critic in one page

The baseline \(V^\pi(s)\) is not something you are handed. An actor-critic method makes it learnable, by training a second network to predict it. The critic \(V_\phi(s)\) is that network — often just an extra output head on the policy's trunk — and it has its own parameter vector \(\phi\), kept deliberately separate from the policy's \(\theta\). Hold onto that separation; the pitfall box above and the .detach() in the code below are both about nothing else. The critic is trained by ordinary regression. You can fit it to the observed returns \(G_t\), or you can bootstrap it — that is, train it toward its own prediction one step ahead, \(r_t + \gamma V_\phi(s_{t+1})\), instead of waiting for the episode to finish. The actor is \(\pi_\theta\) itself, updated by the policy gradient with an advantage estimate \(\hat{A}_t\) in place of the raw return. Figure 2.4 shows how the pieces connect.

The two obvious advantage estimators bracket a spectrum. The Monte Carlo estimate — Monte Carlo meaning simply "use the actual observed return, no shortcuts" — is \(\hat{A}_t = G_t - V(s_t)\). It uses the real return, so it is unbiased, but it carries all the noise of the actual episode. At the other end is the one-step TD residual, \(\hat{A}_t = \delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)\). TD stands for temporal difference: the gap between what the critic predicted for this state and what one real step plus the critic's prediction for the next state say it should have been. That estimator replaces most of the episode with the critic's guess, so it is far quieter, but it is biased by however wrong the critic currently is. GAE, in Chapter 3, interpolates smoothly between the two with a parameter \(\lambda\), and that is the estimator you will actually use.

Two habits from practice are worth naming. Advantages are almost always normalized per batch to zero mean and unit standard deviation; technically that is a batch-computed baseline plus a rescaling — so, like any batch-computed baseline, mildly biased — and it exists to keep the effective step size stable across batches with different reward scales. And an entropy bonus — a small term in the actor loss rewarding the policy for staying stochastic — stops the policy collapsing to one deterministic action before it has explored. In Stable-Baselines3 that is ent_coef. One full iteration:

# one actor-critic iteration (on-policy)
batch   = collect_rollouts(pi_theta, n_steps)        # fresh data, current policy
returns = discounted_returns(batch.rewards, gamma)   # G_t
adv     = returns - V_phi(batch.states)              # or TD / GAE (Chapter 3)
adv     = (adv - adv.mean()) / (adv.std() + 1e-8)    # per-batch normalization
logp    = log_prob(pi_theta, batch.states, batch.actions)
actor_loss  = -(logp * adv.detach()).mean()          # detach: no grad into critic
critic_loss = ((V_phi(batch.states) - returns)**2).mean()
(actor_loss + 0.5 * critic_loss).backward(); opt.step()

Note the phrase fresh data in the first line of the pseudocode. The policy gradient theorem's expectation is taken under the current policy's own trajectory distribution. The moment you take one gradient step, the rollouts you already collected were generated by a different policy \(\pi_{\theta_{old}}\), and reusing them naively biases the gradient. The principled correction is the importance ratio \(\rho_t(\theta) = \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) / \pi_{\theta_{old}}(a_t \mid s_t)\), and Chapter 3 builds PPO around keeping that ratio near 1 so that a limited amount of reuse stays safe. This on-policy constraint — new data for every update — is why the whole family is so sample-hungry: cheap in a simulator running thousands of environments in parallel, brutal on one physical arm. Chapter 4 is the off-policy escape route, and it is the hinge of this book.

On your rig
SB3's PPO on rl-rover is exactly this chapter's actor-critic plus Chapter 3's clip. ActorCriticPolicy is one object holding an actor (a diagonal Gaussian over wheel commands) and a critic (a scalar value head) — separate MLPs by default, a shared trunk only if net_arch says so. This chapter's score functions live in common/policies.py: evaluate_actions() calls distribution.log_prob(actions), and ppo.py forms ratio = th.exp(log_prob - old_log_prob). Put a breakpoint on that log_prob call and you are watching \(\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta\) get assembled, one batch at a time.

2.6 The hidden requirement, and the bridge to Part III

Go back and look at every estimator in this chapter. REINFORCE, the baseline version, the policy gradient theorem, the actor loss in the pseudocode: all contain the same factor, \(\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\). Using any of them means you can evaluate the exact log-density of a sampled action and differentiate it with respect to the weights.

For classical deep RL policies that is trivial. A softmax over discrete actions is an explicit probability vector; take a log and index into it. A diagonal Gaussian — SB3's default for the rover's continuous wheel commands — has a closed-form log-density that fits in five lines:

# diagonal Gaussian policy: log pi(a|s) in closed form
mu, log_std = policy_net(obs)          # network emits mean and log sigma per dim
var  = (2 * log_std).exp()             # sigma squared
logp = -0.5 * (((a - mu) ** 2) / var   # squared-error term, per action dimension
               + 2 * log_std           # the log sigma normalizer
               + math.log(2 * math.pi)).sum(-1)   # sum over action dimensions
logp.backward()                        # autograd now has grad_theta log pi

The requirement is met so cheaply, in every tutorial and every library, that it becomes invisible. Most people who have trained PPO for a year have never once thought of it as a requirement.

It stops being met in Chapter 5. Modern robot policies emit whole action chunks \(a_{t:t+H}\) — a short block of \(H\) future actions produced in one shot — by iteratively transforming random noise, and the network learns a denoiser (diffusion, Chapter 6) or a velocity field (flow matching, Chapter 7) rather than a density. No line of code in such a model computes \(\log \pi_\theta(a_{t:t+H} \mid o)\). The likelihood of a generated chunk is buried inside a multi-step integration path, and it has no closed form of the kind a Gaussian hands you for free.

Be careful how you state this, though, because the strong version — "the gradient cannot be computed at all" — is simply false, and you will meet papers that depend on its being false. The likelihood is not unavailable in principle. For a continuous-time flow you can recover it by integrating along the generation path, accumulating the divergence of the velocity field as you go; and there is a live line of work — you will see it under names like DPPO and Flow-GRPO — that sidesteps the integral entirely by treating the chain of denoising steps as its own small MDP and running PPO on those steps instead. What is true is that all of these are expensive, high-variance, and nothing like the free lunch a Gaussian gives you. In practice \(\log \pi_\theta\) is off the table, and REINFORCE, actor-critic and PPO stall at the same wall for the same reason.

Tractability is also not the only obstacle, and arguably not the most important one. A policy-gradient update does not just push probability mass toward good actions; it pushes mass away from actions that scored badly. For a generative policy whose whole value is that it has learned a narrow manifold of physically coherent action chunks, pushing away is how you shove its predictions off that manifold and get incoherent motion out the other side. Chapter 9 puts the two worlds side by side, covers both failure modes, and works through which parts of your PPO intuition transfer and which do not.

What survives the crash is not the estimator but this chapter's central quantity: the advantage. Once you have \(\hat{A}\), you can weight training data by it (Chapter 4), condition the policy on it as an input (Chapter 10), engineer better estimates of it (Chapter 11), and rank candidate action chunks by it at inference time (Chapter 12). Every one of those is a way of doing policy improvement without ever differentiating a log-probability. The estimator is disposable. The advantage is not. That sentence is the thesis of the rest of this book.

In the LeHome solution
None of this chapter's estimators run on Larchenko's policy. \(\pi_{0.5}\) generates action chunks by flow matching, so \(\log \pi_\theta(a_{t:t+H} \mid o)\) — the term every equation in this chapter differentiates — is not something you can cheaply evaluate, and PPO was off the table from the first day (Larchenko, 2026). The chapter's central quantity survives intact, though: his solution estimates advantages with a success-probability value head \(\hat{p}_{succ}\), GAE, and a damped \(\alpha V\) baseline (Chapter 11), then consumes those advantages through AWR weighting (Chapter 4) and RECAP conditioning (Chapter 10).
Checkpoint
  • Explain to a colleague who has only done supervised learning why you cannot call .backward() on a sum of environment rewards, and why a differentiable simulator does not rescue you.
  • Derive \(\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}[R(\tau) \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(\tau)]\) from the identity \(\nabla_\theta p = p \nabla_\theta \log p\), and say where the transition model drops out and why that makes the method model-free.
  • State the REINFORCE estimator as an English instruction, and name what it does and does not require of your policy.
  • Prove in one line that any action-independent baseline leaves the gradient unbiased, and explain why \(b = V(s)\) turns the weight into an advantage.
  • Work the 100/101 example and the two-action bandit by hand, and use the \(1/\sqrt{N}\) rule to turn a variance reduction into saved episodes on your SO-101.
  • Point to the exact factor in every equation here that stops being available for a flow-matching policy, say why "unavailable in practice" is the accurate claim rather than "impossible in principle", and name the quantity that survives.

Where to go deeper. The original REINFORCE paper is Williams (1992), and it is short and readable. The policy gradient theorem with function approximation is Sutton et al. (1999); Sutton and Barto (2018) covers both with full derivations in its policy-gradient chapter and is the gentlest complete treatment in print. Schulman et al. (2016), the GAE paper, is the sharpest treatment of the bias-variance spectrum that Section 2.5 only sketched, and is the natural bridge into Chapter 3. Appendix A places each of these in a suggested reading order.

Chapter 3 — Trust regions, PPO, and advantage estimation

Chapter 2 left you holding an estimator: push up the log-probability of actions that turned out better than expected, push down the ones that turned out worse, and weight each push by the advantage \(\hat{A}_t\). That is a direction, not a step size. Nothing in Chapter 2 told you how far to move before the estimate you built stops being trustworthy. That question separates a policy gradient that works from one that destroys itself in an afternoon.

You have already run PPO — on your differential-drive rover, through Stable-Baselines3, with a config you probably copied and tweaked. By the end of this chapter you should understand what every one of those knobs was doing, and why the TensorBoard curves looked the way they did.

One thing up front. PPO will not survive the jump to the policies of Part III: flow-matching vision-language-action policies, or VLAs — policies built on a pretrained vision-language model that output robot actions directly (Chapter 8), trained by flow matching, a generative recipe that turns noise into an action along a learned velocity field. Chapter 7 gives the technical reason PPO cannot be used on them; Chapter 9 makes the comparison explicit. The advantage machinery in Section 3.5, however, carries all the way to the LeHome capstone in Chapter 15. If you can only deeply learn one half of this chapter, learn the second half.

3.1 Why step size is the whole game

3.1.1 Supervised learning forgives; reinforcement learning does not

Think about a supervised training run — an image classifier. You take a gradient step that is far too large and the loss jumps. The next minibatch comes from the same fixed dataset, its gradient points back toward the good region, and within a few dozen steps you are roughly where you were. The dataset does not care what your model did.

On-policy reinforcement learning has no such object. The data is the policy. Every state in your next batch was reached because the current policy chose the actions that led there. A destructive update produces a worse policy, which collects worse data, which produces gradients computed on states the good policy would never have visited. The distribution of states you train on moves with every update, and it moves because of your updates.

An analogy. In a self-hosting compiler — one written in the language it compiles — you use version N of the binary to build version N+1. Introduce a subtle code-generation bug and N+1 is slightly wrong. N+1 then builds an N+2 that inherits the bug and adds its own. The corruption compounds because the tool is its own input, exactly as the policy is both the thing being improved and the source of its own training data.

Where the analogy breaks down. With a compiler you have a known-good binary in a bucket, and restoring it costs only the time since the bad commit. Restoring a policy checkpoint costs every environment step collected since — hours in simulation, days on real hardware. And the corruption is statistical, not logical: no diff, no stack trace, often no single step you can blame.

3.1.2 What a collapse actually looks like

The failure mode is stereotyped, so you can recognize it from the plots. In a healthy run ep_rew_mean climbs raggedly; entropy — a measure of how spread out the policy's action distribution still is, unpacked in Section 3.4 — decays gently; and the approximate KL divergence, a running measure of how much an update changed the policy's behavior (made precise in Section 3.3), sits in a narrow band. A collapse announces itself in four curves over two or three rollouts. The approximate KL spikes by an order of magnitude. Entropy either falls off a cliff toward zero or blows upward as the Gaussian's standard deviation diverges. The value loss — the critic's squared prediction error, Section 3.4 — explodes, because the critic's targets moved out from under it. And ep_rew_mean drops to the floor and stays there. The KL spike usually comes first, by a rollout or two. That is why you monitor it: it is the earliest warning that an update is moving further than the data supports.

3.1.3 Why it is often unrecoverable

Why does the reward curve stay flat afterward instead of re-climbing? Suppose your rover had learned to approach the goal region and was collecting the occasional terminal reward. Those near-goal states were in its data, so the critic had learned something about them and the gradient had signal there. After the collapse the rover spins near the spawn point and never reaches the goal again. Those informative states are absent from every later batch.

So the gradient says nothing about them, the critic's estimates for them decay toward the network's default output, and the policy must rediscover the approach behavior by random exploration — often from a policy whose entropy has already collapsed, so it cannot explore.

This is why step size is not a detail you get to postpone. In on-policy RL, controlling how far each update moves the policy is the algorithm. The next three sections are three strategies for one goal: extract as much improvement as possible from a batch without moving so far that the batch stops describing the policy.

3.2 Reusing a batch: importance sampling from scratch

3.2.1 What we want, and the obvious thing to try

Collecting data is expensive. On the rover in simulation a 16,384-step batch takes seconds; on the SO-101 arm it takes minutes of real robot time and human supervision. The vanilla policy gradient from Chapter 2 is wasteful with it: the estimator is valid only at the exact parameters \(\theta_{old}\) that collected the data, so you get one gradient step per batch and then throw the batch away.

The obvious thing to try: do ten gradient steps on the same batch. Why not? The data is right there.

Here is exactly how that fails. After the first step your parameters are no longer \(\theta_{old}\); call them \(\theta_1\). The policy gradient theorem says the gradient of \(J\) is an expectation over actions drawn from the current policy, and your stored actions were drawn from \(\pi_{\theta_{old}}\), not \(\pi_{\theta_1}\). So the second step averages over the wrong distribution — not merely noisy but systematically wrong, and more wrong with each step.

Put that on the rover. The policy is a diagonal Gaussian over wheel commands. At one stored state its mean left-wheel command was \(0.30\) with standard deviation \(0.10\), and the action stored there was \(0.36\) — an unremarkable sample, six tenths of a standard deviation out. Ten unconstrained gradient steps later, the mean for that state has drifted to \(0.16\), so the stored action now sits two standard deviations into the tail: something the current policy would produce about once in forty tries. The gradient does not know that. It keeps pushing on the sample at full weight. Set n_epochs=10 on rl-rover — ten passes over each stored batch — with clipping turned off, and you can watch the consequence: reward climbs for two or three rollouts, then falls to the floor and stays there.

3.2.2 The fix: reweight by how much more likely the new policy is

The repair is importance sampling — estimating an average under one distribution using samples drawn from a different one, by reweighting each sample by the ratio of the two probabilities. Define the importance ratio:

\[ \rho_t(\theta) \;=\; \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a_t \mid s_t)}, \]

where \(\pi_{\theta_{old}}\) is the frozen snapshot of the policy that collected the batch, and \(\pi_\theta\) is the policy as it stands right now, partway through the several passes we are about to take over that batch.

Put numbers on it. Suppose at state \(s_t\) the old policy assigned the action actually taken a probability of \(0.20\), and the current policy assigns it \(0.30\). Then \(\rho_t = 0.30 / 0.20 = 1.5\): the new policy is one and a half times as likely to have produced this sample, so it counts one and a half times as much in the average. Had the new policy dropped to \(0.10\), then \(\rho_t = 0.10/0.20 = 0.5\) and it counts half as much. If the policy has not moved, \(\rho_t = 1\) and nothing changes.

The reason this is exactly right, not merely plausible, is one line of algebra. For any function \(f\) of the action,

\[ \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_{\theta_{old}}}\!\left[ \frac{\pi_\theta(a)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a)} f(a) \right] \;=\; \sum_a \pi_{\theta_{old}}(a)\, \frac{\pi_\theta(a)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a)}\, f(a) \;=\; \sum_a \pi_\theta(a)\, f(a) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_\theta}\!\left[ f(a) \right]. \]

(That display is written with sums, for a discrete action set. For the continuous actions your rover takes, replace \(\sum_a\) with \(\int da\) and read each \(\pi\) as a density rather than a probability; the cancellation is character-for-character identical.)

The \(\pi_{\theta_{old}}\) cancels. Samples from the old policy, weighted by the ratio, give an unbiased average under the new policy. Note what this requires: the actual probability density of the action. In code, \(\rho_t = \exp(\log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) - \log \pi_{\theta_{old}}(a_t \mid s_t))\), in log-space for numerical stability. For a Gaussian policy that log-probability is a closed form you can differentiate. Remember the requirement; Chapter 7 is where it stops being satisfiable.

3.2.3 The surrogate objective and the lie it tells

Plug the ratio into the objective. The result is a surrogate objective — a stand-in we optimize because the thing we actually care about is not directly computable from the data we have:

\[ L(\theta) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_t\!\left[\, \rho_t(\theta)\, \hat{A}_t \,\right] \]
In plain words
The left side, \(L(\theta)\), is the score we push up by changing the policy parameters \(\theta\). The \(\mathbb{E}_t\) means "average over all timesteps in the batch you collected". For one timestep: \(\hat{A}_t\) estimates how much better than average the action taken at time \(t\) turned out to be — positive means better than the policy's own expectation, negative worse. \(\rho_t(\theta)\) is how many times more likely the current policy is to take that same action than the old policy was. Multiplying them says: to raise the score, become more likely to take actions with positive \(\hat{A}_t\) and less likely to take actions with negative \(\hat{A}_t\).

This surrogate has a useful property: at \(\theta = \theta_{old}\), where every \(\rho_t = 1\), its gradient equals the true policy gradient of \(J(\theta)\). Here is why, because it is worth seeing rather than believing. Differentiate the ratio, remembering that \(\pi_{\theta_{old}}(a_t \mid s_t)\) is a stored number, not a function of \(\theta\): \(\nabla_\theta \rho_t = \nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) / \pi_{\theta_{old}}(a_t \mid s_t)\). Evaluate that at \(\theta = \theta_{old}\), where the denominator is the numerator's own probability, and apply the identity \(\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta = \pi_\theta \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta\) from Chapter 2. The \(\pi_\theta\) cancels, leaving \(\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\), so the surrogate's gradient is \(\mathbb{E}_t[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\, \hat{A}_t]\) — the score-function estimator you built in Chapter 2. PPO's first gradient step on a fresh batch and REINFORCE-with-a-baseline's step are the same step. Everything PPO adds is about the steps after it.

Ascending the surrogate therefore starts out exactly correct. But it is only a local approximation, and you should know precisely which part is a lie. The ratio corrects for the new policy choosing different actions at the states in your batch. It does nothing about the new policy visiting different states. The surrogate quietly assumes the state distribution is frozen at whatever \(\pi_{\theta_{old}}\) produced.

Think of an A/B test on a web service. You ran variant B on 20% of traffic and now want to estimate what happens at 30%. Reweighting your logged sessions is reasonable. But if variant B also changes which users come back tomorrow, your reweighted logs describe a population that no longer exists. Where the analogy breaks down: in an A/B test that drift is slow and you can re-measure. In RL it happens inside one training iteration, and the next batch is already coming from the drifted policy.

So the further \(\rho_t\) strays from 1, the bigger the lie. Sections 3.3 and 3.4 are two mechanisms for ascending \(L(\theta)\) while keeping \(\rho_t\) near 1.

3.3 TRPO in one section

3.3.1 The constrained problem

Trust Region Policy Optimization (Schulman et al., 2015) takes the honest route. If the surrogate is only trustworthy near \(\theta_{old}\), say so explicitly: maximize \(L(\theta)\) subject to a hard constraint that the average KL divergence between \(\pi_{\theta_{old}}\) and \(\pi_\theta\), taken over the states in the batch, stays below a small threshold such as \(0.01\).

The region of parameter space where that constraint holds is the trust region: the neighborhood in which you trust your approximation. Inside it, improving the surrogate provably improves a lower bound on the true objective \(J(\theta)\). That is a real guarantee, and more than PPO can claim.

3.3.2 KL divergence in plain words

KL divergence measures how different two distributions are, and the definition \(D_{KL}(p \,\|\, q) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p}[\log p(x) - \log q(x)]\) is not illuminating on its own. Bind the symbols first: \(p\) is the old policy \(\pi_{\theta_{old}}\), \(q\) is the new policy \(\pi_\theta\), and \(\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p}\) says the average is taken over actions drawn the way the old policy would draw them. The useful intuition: how surprised is the old policy by the new one? If the two agree everywhere, every log-difference is zero and the KL is zero. If the new policy has taken mass away from actions the old one considered likely, those are precisely the actions you keep drawing; each one has \(\log p\) large and \(\log q\) small, so the log-differences are large and positive and the KL grows. Moving mass onto actions the old policy never took barely registers directly — you almost never draw those actions, so they almost never enter the average. It registers because that mass had to come from somewhere.

It is not symmetric — \(D_{KL}(p\|q) \ne D_{KL}(q\|p)\) in general — and it is not a distance. For our purposes it is a scalar that reads zero when the policy has not moved and grows as it does, in units that reflect the shape of the distribution rather than the size of the parameter change. That distinction matters: two policies can have very different parameters and behave identically. KL measures behavior, not parameters.

3.3.3 Why almost nobody runs TRPO

The implementation is where it falls apart. Enforcing the constraint exactly requires a second-order object: the Fisher information matrix, which is the curvature of the KL at \(\theta_{old}\) — a statement of how fast behavior changes per unit of parameter change. For a network with millions of parameters you cannot even store that matrix. So TRPO never forms it. It computes only the matrix's product with one vector at a time (a Fisher-vector product, obtainable from a pair of backward passes), solves for the step direction with conjugate gradient — an iterative linear solver that needs nothing but such products — and then backtracks, halving the proposed step repeatedly, until the KL constraint really holds.

That is three pieces of nontrivial numerical machinery around every update. It is slow, fiddly to get right, and interacts badly with architectures that share a trunk between policy and value function. TRPO's lasting contribution is the framing: a policy update as constrained optimization over a trust region. The practical tool arrived two years later with none of the machinery.

3.4 PPO: clip the surrogate

3.4.1 The clipped objective

Proximal Policy Optimization (Schulman et al., 2017) asks a different question: instead of forbidding large steps, what if we stop paying for them? If moving \(\rho_t\) beyond a small interval around 1 earns no extra objective value, plain gradient ascent has no reason to go there.

\[ L^{\mathrm{CLIP}}(\theta) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_t\!\left[\, \min\!\Big( \rho_t(\theta)\, \hat{A}_t,\;\; \mathrm{clip}\big(\rho_t(\theta),\, 1-\epsilon,\, 1+\epsilon\big)\, \hat{A}_t \Big) \right] \]
In plain words
For each timestep in the batch, compute two numbers. The first is the plain surrogate term \(\rho_t \hat{A}_t\) from Section 3.2, where \(\hat{A}_t\) is the advantage estimate and \(\rho_t\) the importance ratio. The second is the same product, but with the ratio first squashed into the window \([1-\epsilon,\, 1+\epsilon\,]\): \(\mathrm{clip}\) returns \(1-\epsilon\) if \(\rho_t\) is below it, \(1+\epsilon\) if above, \(\rho_t\) unchanged in between. The clip parameter \(\epsilon\), typically 0.1 to 0.3, sets the window's width. Then take \(\min\) of the two — whichever is worse for us — and average over the batch. Preferring the smaller of an honest estimate and a capped one is what makes the objective refuse to reward large moves.

The \(\min\) wrapped around the \(\mathrm{clip}\) is the part everyone finds confusing at first, and the confusion is legitimate: two nested operations that look like they do the same job. They do not. Unpack it one sign of the advantage at a time, following Figure 3.1 as you go.

3.4.2 Case one: the advantage was positive

\(\hat{A}_t \gt 0\) means the action turned out better than the policy expected, so we want to raise its probability — we want \(\rho_t\) above 1. As it grows, the unclipped term \(\rho_t \hat{A}_t\) grows linearly, and the clipped term grows with it until \(\rho_t\) hits \(1+\epsilon\), where it freezes at \((1+\epsilon)\hat{A}_t\). Past that point the clipped term is the smaller of the two, the \(\min\) selects it, and the objective is flat.

Flat means zero gradient. Once the current policy assigns this action \(1+\epsilon\) times its old probability, this sample stops pushing at all. With \(\epsilon = 0.2\): raise it by 20%, then stop. The sample has said what it has to say.

3.4.3 Case two: the advantage was negative

\(\hat{A}_t \lt 0\) means the action was worse than expected, so we want \(\rho_t\) below 1. Because \(\hat{A}_t\) is negative, shrinking \(\rho_t\) makes \(\rho_t \hat{A}_t\) less negative, which improves the objective. That improvement stops at \(\rho_t = 1-\epsilon\), where the clipped term freezes at \((1-\epsilon)\hat{A}_t\); below that the clipped term is the more negative of the two, the \(\min\) selects it, and the gradient dies again.

Now the interesting half. What if \(\rho_t\) goes up instead — if an earlier minibatch update in this same epoch accidentally raised the probability of an action we know was bad? Then \(\rho_t \hat{A}_t\) grows more and more negative with no cap, and the \(\min\) selects that unclipped branch. The mistake is punished at full strength, with no ceiling.

3.4.4 The asymmetry is the entire point

Look at Figure 3.1 as a pair. The incentive to improve is capped; the penalty for getting worse is not. That asymmetry is what the \(\min\) buys, and it is why the objective is called pessimistic. If you simply clipped \(\rho_t\) and multiplied, a sample whose probability had been wrongly pushed up would contribute nothing, and the mistake would go uncorrected.

Be clear about what this is not. It is an incentive structure, not a constraint. Nothing in \(L^{\mathrm{CLIP}}\) makes it impossible to leave the window: a large learning rate, or too many passes over one batch, can carry \(\theta\) far past \(1 \pm \epsilon\), because a sample's gradient vanishes only once you are already outside. That is why you still monitor the KL.

3.4.5 The full loss, and one iteration of code

Because the clip keeps updates near \(\pi_{\theta_{old}}\), PPO can safely reuse a batch: collect a rollout of \(N\) steps from several parallel environments, then run several epochs — complete passes over the stored batch — of minibatch gradient descent before collecting fresh data. That reuse is where most of PPO's sample efficiency comes from. The policy term is not the whole loss, though:

\[ L^{\mathrm{PPO}}(\theta,\phi) \;=\; -\,L^{\mathrm{CLIP}}(\theta) \;+\; c_v\, \mathbb{E}_t\!\left[\big(V_\phi(s_t) - \hat{G}_t\big)^2\right] \;-\; c_e\, \mathbb{E}_t\!\left[\mathcal{H}\big(\pi_\theta(\cdot \mid s_t)\big)\right] \]
In plain words
This is what the optimizer minimizes, so signs flip relative to the objective. \(\theta\) are the policy's parameters, \(\phi\) the critic's. The first term is minus the clipped surrogate: minimizing it maximizes \(L^{\mathrm{CLIP}}\). The second is the value loss — squared error between the critic's prediction \(V_\phi(s_t)\) and the observed return target \(\hat{G}_t\) — which trains the critic the advantage estimator needs. The third is the entropy bonus: \(\mathcal{H}\) is the entropy of the action distribution, high when the policy is spread out, near zero when nearly deterministic. It enters with a minus sign, so minimizing the loss increases entropy, paying the policy to stay random. \(c_v\) and \(c_e\) are scalar weights, commonly 0.5 and 0.01.

Where does \(\hat{G}_t\) come from? Not from a second pass over the episode. Once Section 3.5 hands you \(\hat{A}_t\), the target is just \(\hat{G}_t = \hat{A}_t + V(s_t)\) — the critic's own estimate, corrected by the advantage you measured. That identity is what makes the critic loss and the advantage estimator one machine instead of two, and it is what fills the returns field below (and rollout_buffer.returns in Stable-Baselines3).

# One PPO iteration: collect once, then reuse the batch several times.
batch = collect_rollout(pi_old, n_envs=8, n_steps=2048)   # 16384 steps total
adv   = gae(batch.rewards, batch.values, gamma, lam)      # Section 3.5
batch.returns = adv + batch.values                        # critic targets: G = A + V
batch.adv     = (adv - adv.mean()) / (adv.std() + 1e-8)   # per-batch normalization
for epoch in range(4):                                    # 4 passes over the SAME data
    for mb in minibatches(batch, size=512):
        # ratio in log-space; mb.logp_old was stored during collection,
        # so no frozen copy of the old network is needed here
        rho   = exp(logp(pi, mb.a) - mb.logp_old)
        # min() of unclipped and clipped: take the pessimistic branch
        l_pi  = -min(rho * mb.adv,
                     clip(rho, 1-eps, 1+eps) * mb.adv).mean()
        l_v   = (v(mb.s) - mb.returns).pow(2).mean()      # critic regression
        loss  = l_pi + 0.5 * l_v - 0.01 * entropy(pi, mb.s)
        loss.backward(); opt.step(); opt.zero_grad()
pi_old = pi                                               # snapshot for the next iteration

PPO became the field's default for an unglamorous reason: it is a first-order method, roughly a dozen lines on top of an actor-critic, robust across a wide range of hyperparameters, and it scales by adding parallel environments. It gives up TRPO's guarantees and keeps most of its results.

But notice what it needs. Every line above depends on an exact, differentiable \(\log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\) for each sampled action. Chapter 7 shows that flow-matching VLAs cannot provide one, and Chapter 9 works through the consequences side by side with everything here. That single missing quantity is why the LeHome solution left PPO behind entirely.

Words you will hear
Clip fraction — the fraction of samples in a minibatch where \(\rho_t\) fell outside \([1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon]\). Approximate KL (approx_kl) — a cheap sample estimate of the KL between old and new policy, used for monitoring and early stopping. Explained variance — \(1 - \mathrm{Var}(\hat{G}-V)/\mathrm{Var}(\hat{G})\); near 1 means a useful critic, near or below 0 a useless one. Adaptive KL penalty — the other PPO variant from the same paper: subtract \(\beta_{KL} D_{KL}\) from the objective you maximize, equivalently add \(+\beta_{KL} D_{KL}\) to the loss you minimize, with \(\beta_{KL}\) retuned between iterations to hold the measured KL near a target. The subscript keeps it apart from the AWR temperature \(\beta\) later in the book. Rarely used today. Epoch / minibatch — one full pass over the stored rollout, and one slice of it.

3.5 Advantage estimation: from Monte Carlo to TD to GAE

The clipped objective consumes \(\hat{A}_t\) and does nothing to check it. Whatever quality that estimate has, the learning inherits. So where does it come from? Two pure answers exist, and they fail in opposite directions.

3.5.1 Monte Carlo: unbiased and nearly unusable

The direct approach: run the episode to the end, add up the discounted rewards you actually received, subtract the baseline. That is \(\hat{A}_t = G_t - V(s_t)\) with \(G_t = \sum_k \gamma^k r_{t+k}\). Nothing is approximated — \(G_t\) is what happened. The estimate is unbiased.

Here is the concrete failure. On your rover, consider the first action of an episode, a small steering command. Two episodes start from nearly the same state and take nearly the same first action. In one, the randomized obstacle layout leaves a clear lane and the rover reaches the goal for \(G_0 = +180\). In the other an obstacle sits square in the path, the rover detours, runs out of time, and \(G_0 = -20\). The same action is scored at \(+180\) in one sample and \(-20\) in the other, and the difference has nothing to do with the action. \(G_t\) sums every random event between \(t\) and the end of the episode and charges all of it to \(a_t\). The variance is enormous and grows with episode length.

3.5.2 TD: low variance and wrong

The opposite approach: do not wait. Take one real reward, then ask the critic what everything after is worth. That gives the TD residual, the one-step temporal-difference error:

\[ \delta_t \;=\; r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t). \]

In words: the immediate reward, plus the discounted value the critic assigns to where you landed, minus the value it assigned to where you started. If the transition went better than the critic expected, \(\delta_t\) is positive. Only one step of real randomness enters, so variance is small and does not grow with the episode.

Here is its concrete failure. Early in training your critic is a barely-trained network outputting numbers near zero everywhere. Your rover takes the action that turns it toward the goal, moving from a state genuinely worth \(0.9\) to one genuinely worth \(0.95\). The reward on this step is \(0\), because reward is sparse. The critic reports \(V(s_t) = 0.02\) and \(V(s_{t+1}) = 0.01\). Then \(\delta_t = 0 + 0.99 \times 0.01 - 0.02 = -0.01\): slightly negative. The estimator says a good action was mildly bad. That is not noise you can average away — run it a thousand times and the sign stays wrong, because the error lives in \(V\), not in the sampling. That is bias.

A software analogy: MC times a request end-to-end with a stopwatch; TD reads a cost estimate off a cached model of how long each function takes. The stopwatch is honest, but every measurement is polluted by whatever else the machine was doing. The cost model is stable and, if stale, gives the same wrong number every time. Where it breaks down: a profiler's cost model is calibrated independently of the request you are timing, while the critic is trained on the very returns you are estimating, so its errors and your data's errors are correlated.

3.5.3 The dial between them

Between the extremes sit \(k\)-step estimators: sum \(k\) real rewards, then bootstrap with \(\gamma^k V(s_{t+k})\). Larger \(k\) means more real signal and more variance; smaller \(k\) means more reliance on the critic and more bias. Picking a single \(k\) is a brittle decision. Generalized Advantage Estimation (Schulman et al., 2016) sidesteps it by blending all values of \(k\) at once with exponentially decaying weights:

\[ \hat{A}_t^{\mathrm{GAE}(\gamma,\lambda)} \;=\; \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} (\gamma\lambda)^l\, \delta_{t+l}, \qquad \delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t). \]
In plain words
To score the action at time \(t\), walk forward through the rest of the episode collecting TD residuals: \(\delta_t\) from this step, \(\delta_{t+1}\) from the next, and so on, where each \(\delta\) is the reward \(r\) plus the discounted next value minus the current one. \(l\) counts how many steps ahead you have walked. Each residual is multiplied by \((\gamma\lambda)^l\), a number below 1 raised to the \(l\)-th power, so residuals further ahead count exponentially less. \(\gamma\) is the discount from the problem definition; \(\lambda\), the GAE parameter, lies in \([0,1]\) and sets how fast that decay happens. At \(\lambda = 0\) only the first term survives: pure TD. At \(\lambda = 1\) nothing decays beyond \(\gamma\) and the sum telescopes into \(G_t - V(s_t)\): pure Monte Carlo. Everything between is a blend.

Figure 3.2 draws \(\lambda\) as the dial it is. In practice \(\lambda \approx 0.95\) sits close to the MC end. Read it as: trust the real rewards for roughly the next twenty steps, then hand off to the critic. Note also that the implementation is one backward pass, not an infinite sum — accumulate \(\hat{A}_t = \delta_t + \gamma\lambda \hat{A}_{t+1}\) from the end of the rollout to the start, which costs essentially nothing.

3.5.4 \(\gamma\) and \(\lambda\) are not the same knob

They look alike in the formula, they multiply together, and both are slightly below 1. Everything else about them differs, and conflating them is a common confusion.

\(\gamma\) belongs to the problem definition. It is part of the return \(G_t\) you decided to maximize back in Chapter 1, and it says how much the agent should care about a reward twenty seconds from now relative to one right now. Change \(\gamma\) and you change what the optimal policy is: a \(\gamma = 0.9\) rover is a more impatient animal than a \(\gamma = 0.999\) rover, and the two behave differently at convergence. Tune \(\gamma\) to the task's time horizon.

\(\lambda\) belongs to the estimator only and appears nowhere in the objective. It trades bias against variance in the numbers you feed the gradient, and with a perfect critic every \(\lambda\) estimates the same quantity with different noise; the optimal policy is unchanged. Tune \(\lambda\) to how much you trust your critic — young critic or sparse reward, push it up; well-fit critic and long noisy episodes, pull it down.

3.5.5 Worked example: three estimators, one three-step episode

Take a deliberately tiny episode so every number is checkable by hand. Three steps; \(\gamma = 0.9\); rewards \(r_0 = 0\), \(r_1 = 0\), \(r_2 = 1\) — success only at the end, the sparse-reward situation you face on a robot. The critic, mid-training and mediocre, reports \(V(s_0) = 0.5\), \(V(s_1) = 0.6\), \(V(s_2) = 0.7\), and \(V(s_3) = 0\) because \(s_3\) is terminal.

First the three TD residuals, \(\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)\), every multiplication shown:

\[ \delta_0 = 0 + 0.9 \times 0.6 - 0.5 = 0 + 0.54 - 0.5 = 0.04 \]

\[ \delta_1 = 0 + 0.9 \times 0.7 - 0.6 = 0 + 0.63 - 0.6 = 0.03 \]

\[ \delta_2 = 1 + 0.9 \times 0 - 0.7 = 1 + 0 - 0.7 = 0.30 \]

With \(\lambda = 0\) the sum keeps only its first term, so the advantages are the residuals themselves: \(\hat{A}_0 = 0.04\), \(\hat{A}_1 = 0.03\), \(\hat{A}_2 = 0.30\). Read what that says. The success at \(t=2\) gives a healthy signal for the last action, but the first action gets \(0.04\) — almost nothing. The estimator refuses to look past one step; it credits the first action only for the critic's opinion that \(s_1\) beats \(s_0\), and that opinion is worth \(0.04\).

With \(\lambda = 0.95\) the decay factor is \(\gamma\lambda = 0.9 \times 0.95 = 0.855\), and we accumulate backward from the end:

A_2 = d_2                        = 0.30
A_1 = d_1 + 0.855 * A_2
    = 0.03 + 0.855 * 0.30
    = 0.03 + 0.2565             = 0.2865   ~  0.287
A_0 = d_0 + 0.855 * A_1
    = 0.04 + 0.855 * 0.2865
    = 0.04 + 0.24496            = 0.28496  ~  0.285

Read this one too. The terminal success now reaches the first action almost undamped: \(0.285\) versus \(0.04\), same action, same data, same critic. That is a factor of just over seven in the learning signal — \(0.285 / 0.04 = 7.125\) — and the only thing that changed was one number in the config file.

With \(\lambda = 1\) the decay factor is \(\gamma \lambda = 0.9 \times 1 = 0.9\), giving \(\hat{A}_1 = 0.03 + 0.9 \times 0.30 = 0.03 + 0.27 = 0.30\) and \(\hat{A}_0 = 0.04 + 0.9 \times 0.30 = 0.04 + 0.27 = 0.31\). Check that against the Monte Carlo definition: \(G_0 = 0 + 0.9 \times 0 + 0.9^2 \times 1 = 0.81\), so \(\hat{A}_0 = G_0 - V(s_0) = 0.81 - 0.5 = 0.31\). The two routes agree — the telescoping property in action.

So \(\lambda = 0.95\) recovers \(0.285\) of the \(0.31\) full Monte Carlo gives, while still damping the far tail. On a three-step episode that damping buys little; on a 500-step episode it is the difference between a usable signal and noise. Figure 3.3 puts all three side by side.

3.6 PPO in practice on the rover

Everything so far has been mechanism. This section is what you actually do with it on rl-rover: a starting configuration, and the four plots that tell you whether the run is healthy.

3.6.1 A configuration to start from

On a task the size of rl-rover, a sane configuration is 8 parallel environments, 2048 steps each per rollout (a 16,384-step batch), 4 epochs of minibatch updates, \(\gamma = 0.99\), \(\lambda = 0.95\), \(\epsilon = 0.2\), and a budget of roughly 5M environment steps. Those are numbers to start from, not numbers to tune first. Two of them repay a second look. The 4 epochs are the reuse factor of Section 3.4: raise it and you extract more from each batch, but you also travel further from \(\pi_{\theta_{old}}\) within one iteration. The \(\lambda = 0.95\) is the dial of Section 3.5, sitting near the Monte Carlo end because your critic starts out untrained.

3.6.2 The four curves

Four TensorBoard curves tell you nearly everything. Read them as a set; their failure modes are joint.

Episode reward (ep_rew_mean) is the ground truth. Everything else exists to explain this curve. If it is going up, resist the urge to fix things.

Approximate KL and clip fraction tell you how far updates actually move the policy. Healthy is a KL in the \(0.01\)–\(0.03\) band with clip fraction around \(0.1\)–\(0.3\). Clip fraction near zero means the clip never binds: either the learning rate is too timid or learning has converged, and the reward curve tells you which. KL spiking with clip fraction above \(0.4\) is the danger sign of Section 3.1. Lower the learning rate, or cut the epochs per batch.

Value loss should fall early, then track changes in reward rather than sitting flat. If it stays large, check explained variance: a critic near zero there contributes bias and nothing else.

Entropy should decay slowly and smoothly. A cliff-drop in the first 10% of training means the policy went deterministic before it found anything worth being confident about; raise the entropy coefficient. Entropy that climbs steadily usually means a broken advantage signal.

On your rig
In Stable-Baselines3 these knobs are n_envs, n_steps, n_epochs, clip_range, gae_lambda, ent_coef; the curves are approx_kl, clip_fraction, entropy_loss, value_loss, explained_variance. Re-run rl-rover and watch clip_fraction during the reward ramp — it rises exactly when the policy changes fastest, the most direct view of this chapter you will get. If a sim-to-real transfer got worse after a "better" run, check whether entropy collapsed early; overconfident policies randomize poorly and transfer poorly. Your hil-serl SO-101 setup uses an off-policy learner, so there is no clip_fraction there, but the critic diagnostics carry over.
Pitfalls
Two silent killers. (1) Skipping per-batch advantage normalization: raw \(\hat{A}\) magnitudes drift over training, so the effective learning rate drifts with them. Normalize advantages to zero mean and unit variance per batch — but never normalize rewards mid-run with running statistics you later change, or the critic's targets shift underneath it. (2) Reward scaling: multiplying rewards by 100 multiplies the value loss by 10,000 and its gradients by 100. If the value loss dwarfs the policy loss, the shared trunk trains the critic and ignores the actor; rescale the rewards or lower the value coefficient \(c_v\).
In the LeHome solution
PPO never appears. A flow-matching VLA has no tractable \(\log \pi_\theta(a \mid o)\), so the ratio \(\rho_t\) simply cannot be computed (Chapter 7; Chapter 9 makes the comparison explicit). But Section 3.5 survives completely intact. Larchenko's advantage pipeline uses TD residuals, Monte Carlo returns, and GAE computed over checkpoint rewards, with the learned success-probability head \(\hat{p}_{succ}\) standing in for \(V\). Because that value estimate is imperfect, the full subtraction is replaced by a damped baseline \(\alpha V\), where the damping coefficient \(\alpha\) sits below 1 and deliberately subtracts less than the whole value estimate (Chapter 11). The estimator outlived the algorithm that made it famous (Larchenko, 2026).
Checkpoint
  • Explain why one oversized update can permanently damage an on-policy run, and name the TensorBoard signatures of a policy collapse.
  • Compute the importance ratio \(\rho_t\) from two probabilities, and say which part of the surrogate objective is an approximation and why it degrades as \(\rho_t\) leaves 1.
  • Show that at \(\theta = \theta_{old}\) the surrogate's gradient is Chapter 2's score-function estimator.
  • Walk through \(L^{\mathrm{CLIP}}\) case by case for \(\hat{A}_t \gt 0\) and \(\hat{A}_t \lt 0\), and say why the objective is deliberately asymmetric.
  • Write down the three terms of the full PPO loss and say what each is for.
  • Compute GAE by hand from a short list of rewards and critic values, and say why \(\gamma\) changes the optimal policy while \(\lambda\) changes only the noise in your estimate of it.

Where to go deeper. The primary sources are short and unusually readable: Schulman et al. (2015) for TRPO, Schulman et al. (2016) for GAE, Schulman et al. (2017) for PPO. For the gap between the paper and code that actually trains, Engstrom et al. (2020) and Andrychowicz et al. (2021) dissect which implementation details in on-policy RL matter and which are folklore — read at least one before you tune anything. Appendix A places all three primary papers in a suggested reading order.

Part II

Learning from data you already have

Real robots make samples expensive. This part rebuilds RL as a weighted supervised problem — the form that survives everything that follows.

Chapter 4 — RL as weighted behavior cloning

Chapter 3 ended with PPO: a robust on-policy algorithm that improves a policy using data the policy itself just generated. This chapter takes the opposite road. It starts from supervised learning on demonstrations, asks how to turn that into reinforcement learning, and arrives at an update so simple it fits on one line: clone the data, but weight each sample by how good its action turned out to be.

That one line — advantage-weighted regression — is the load-bearing idea of this entire book. Not because it is the most powerful algorithm here; it is not. It is load-bearing because it is the form of RL that survives when the policy stops being a small Gaussian network and becomes a large generative model. Everything in Part III depends on this chapter, so it is worth going slowly.

Here is the route. We price out why on-policy learning is a bad fit for real hardware (4.1), try the obvious alternative and watch it break (4.2), retreat to plain behavior cloning, which cannot break that way but has a hard ceiling (4.3), and then fix the ceiling without giving up the safety: that fix is AWR (4.4). AWAC is a variation on the theme (4.5), and 4.6 states the property that makes the whole book hang together.

4.1 The robot-data reality

4.1.1 What we want, and the obvious thing to try

We want a policy on a physical arm that gets better with experience. You already know a method that does this and have personally made it work: PPO on your differential-drive rover. So the obvious move is to point it at the SO-101.

Before you do, price it out. PPO is on-policy, meaning it can only learn from data generated by the current policy (or something extremely close to it): each batch is collected, used for a handful of gradient epochs, and then discarded, because the importance ratio \(\rho_t(\theta)\) only corrects for small policy drift. Suppose you budget a modest run of one million environment steps — small by simulation standards; your rover runs used more. Two rates show up in this chapter and both are real: you log teleoperation through the leader arm at 20 Hz, and you run the policy autonomously at 30 Hz. At the autonomous rate, an episode of 20 seconds is 600 steps, so one million steps is about 1,667 episodes.

Now add the part simulation does not have: the reset. After each episode a human has to re-flatten the cloth, or re-place the cube, or untangle a cable. Call it 15 seconds, which is optimistic. Each episode therefore costs 20 + 15 = 35 seconds of wall clock, and:

\[ \frac{1{,}000{,}000}{600} \approx 1{,}667 \ \text{episodes}, \qquad 1{,}667 \times 35\ \text{s} = 58{,}345\ \text{s}, \qquad \frac{58{,}345}{3600} \approx 16.2\ \text{hours}. \]

Sixteen hours for one run. Five seeds, the minimum anyone would accept in a paper, is 81 hours — two working weeks of a person standing next to a moving arm, and that is before anything on the arm wears out.

4.1.2 How it fails, and the fix

The deeper problem is not the hours. It is that on-policy learning throws the hours away. After the update, that motion is formally worthless for the next update: the policy has moved, so the data is off-distribution, and PPO's clipping machinery exists precisely to stop you from using it too hard. You are renting your data, not owning it.

Meanwhile, look at what is sitting on your disk. Your rl-rover PPO runs saved rollouts at every checkpoint. Your hil-serl replay buffers hold hours of SO-101 experience: teleoperation demonstrations, Xbox-pad interventions (in your first working run, 98% of frames were interventions), and autonomous rollouts from a dozen policy versions. None of it came from your current policy. All of it is real physics, real cameras, real outcomes.

Learning about a policy \(\pi_\theta\) from data generated by some other policy is called off-policy learning. Learning entirely from a fixed logged dataset, with no environment interaction at all during training, is offline RL. The policy that actually generated the data — whatever it was — is the behavior policy, written \(\pi_\beta\). Demonstrations are just the special case where \(\pi_\beta\) is a competent human holding the leader arm.

Why should this work at all? Because nothing about the data's origin makes its content less true. When your old checkpoint commanded a gripper close at a particular wrist angle and the cloth slipped, the slipping was real; physics does not care which network emitted the command. The hard part — and it is genuinely hard — is extracting that information without fooling yourself.

Words you will hear

Off-policy. Learning about one policy from data generated by another. Offline RL (older papers: batch RL). Training on a fixed dataset with zero environment interaction. Behavior policy \(\pi_\beta\). Whatever produced the data: a human, a scripted controller, an old checkpoint, or a mixture. Distributional shift. The gap between the state-action distribution in your data and the one your new policy will actually visit; actions outside the data's coverage are called OOD (out-of-distribution). Conservatism / pessimism. The family of fixes — conservative Q-learning (CQL) and implicit Q-learning (IQL) — that deliberately push value estimates down on unseen actions, or refuse to evaluate them at all. Temperature. A scalar dividing something before an exponential, controlling how sharply the result concentrates.

4.2 Offline RL's failure mode

4.2.1 The obvious thing to try, again

You have the pile. The obvious move is to run a standard off-policy algorithm on it — a Q-learning-style actor-critic. Train a critic \(Q(s,a)\) on the logged transitions by temporal-difference regression, then train the actor to output the action that maximizes the critic. No environment interaction needed. This is the structure of the algorithms in your hil-serl setup, minus the part where fresh data keeps arriving. It does not work, and the way it fails explains the design of every method in this chapter.

4.2.2 Exactly how it fails

Make it concrete. Your buffer contains SO-101 wrist-flex commands, and because a human generated them through a leader arm at 20 Hz, the per-step wrist delta is always somewhere in \([-10^\circ, +10^\circ]\). Nothing in the dataset has a delta of \(+60^\circ\). Not one frame.

Now ask the critic what \(Q(s, +60^\circ)\) is. The critic is a neural network. It will answer. It has no mechanism for saying "I have never seen that." It extrapolates smoothly, and the number it returns is whatever the network's shape happens to produce out there. Suppose the true returns in your task all lie in \([0, 1]\) (say, success probability), but the critic's surface happens to peak at \(Q(s, +60^\circ) = 8.5\).

Now run the actor update. The actor's job is to find the action maximizing \(Q\). It is a gradient-based optimizer with one objective: climb. It will find that peak, because the peak is exactly what it is searching for. This is the crucial asymmetry: extrapolation error is random in sign, but the optimizer specifically hunts for the positive errors. The policy walks toward \(+60^\circ\), the arm slams the wrist over, and nothing in the training loop ever contradicts it, because offline there is no environment to send back the bad news.

It gets worse, because of bootstrapping — the fact that a value estimate is trained against a target built out of other value estimates rather than out of observed returns. The TD target for a logged transition is \(r_t + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1}, a')\), where \(a'\) is any action you could take at the next state \(s_{t+1}\), and that maximum is taken over the same inflated surface. So the fantasy value at \(+60^\circ\) gets copied into the target for the previous state, and then the state before that. A few sweeps through the buffer and the whole value function has drifted upward, anchored to an action that never existed. Everyone who runs vanilla off-policy RL on static data sees this at least once: the loss curves look fine, the values look great, the robot is nonsense.

In plain words

The critic takes a state \(s\) and an action \(a\) and returns a number: how much total future reward you expect if you take \(a\) here and then behave as usual. The dataset pins that number down only where data exists. Everywhere else it is a guess dressed up as a measurement. The actor is a search procedure over \(a\). Search plus unpinned guesses equals the search finding the guesses. Offline, no feedback loop closes.

A software analogy: a neural critic is like reading past the end of an array in C. There is no bounds check and no exception — you get a plausible-looking number back and the program keeps running. Where the analogy breaks down: an out-of-bounds read returns random garbage, so you usually notice fast. Neural extrapolation returns something smooth and confident, and because the optimizer selects for the highest such values, the errors you chase are systematically the flattering ones. The failure is quieter and better disguised than a memory bug.

4.2.3 The fix, and why it works

Every method that succeeds at offline RL applies the same medicine in a different flavor: keep the policy close to the data. Some add an explicit penalty on the divergence between \(\pi_\theta\) and \(\pi_\beta\). Conservative Q-learning (CQL) trains the critic to actively push values down on actions the policy proposes but the data does not contain. Implicit Q-learning (IQL) avoids ever evaluating \(Q\) at an action outside the dataset. It works for one reason: the queries you make are then queries the data can answer, so the asymmetry that generated the disaster has nothing left to exploit.

The family we build in this chapter enforces that constraint in the most literal way available. AWR, the method of 4.4, never evaluates the policy at an action of its own choosing at all — it only ever looks at actions physically present in the dataset, because it refuses to leave the supervised-learning template. (Its cousin AWAC, in 4.5, does reintroduce a critic and does query it at self-chosen actions; 4.5 explains what makes that survivable. Read 4.4 first.) The supervised-learning template is where we go next.

4.3 Behavior cloning as the base case

4.3.1 The obvious thing to try, one more time

Behavior cloning (BC) treats control as ordinary supervised learning: collect observation–action pairs \((o_i, a_i)\) from a demonstrator and fit a network to predict the action from the observation. As an objective,

\[ \max_\theta \; \sum_i \log \pi_\theta(a_i \mid o_i), \]

In plain words

\(\pi_\theta(a \mid o)\) is the probability density the network, with parameters \(\theta\), assigns to action \(a\) after seeing observation \(o\) — on your rig, \(o\) is a pair of camera frames plus the joint positions. \(a_i\) and \(o_i\) are the action and observation recorded on frame \(i\), and the sum runs over every frame you logged. The logarithm turns a product of per-frame probabilities into a sum you can minibatch. Maximizing that sum over \(\theta\) means: make the recorded actions the ones the network would most likely have produced. And notice what is absent — there is no reward anywhere in this expression.

Or, for a deterministic policy that outputs one action rather than a distribution, minimize a mean-squared error between the predicted and recorded actions. That is the whole method. There is no reward, no value function, no exploration, no critic, no environment.

What BC inherits from supervised learning is exactly what makes deep learning pleasant: it is stable, the loss goes down most of the time, it scales with data and parameters, and it works with any architecture you can backpropagate through. Nothing in the recipe cares whether \(\pi_\theta\) is a two-layer MLP or a three-billion-parameter transformer. Hold on to that sentence; it is the one this chapter is ultimately about.

4.3.2 Exactly how it falls short

Its ceiling is just as easy to state: BC treats every action in the dataset as equally worth imitating. It clones the demonstrator's mistakes with exactly the same fidelity as their successes.

Make that concrete. Say you record 40 teleop episodes of a grasp on the SO-101. In 12 of them you fumbled the approach and spent about three seconds scrabbling at the object before recovering. At 20 Hz that is 60 frames each, so those episodes contribute roughly 720 frames of scrabbling to a dataset with perhaps 8,000 frames near the grasp. Maximum likelihood does not know scrabbling was a mistake. It sees that from observations that look like "gripper near object," the recorded behavior is a clean grasp most of the time and a scrabble about 9% of the time, and it dutifully reproduces that mixture. You did not train a policy that grasps; you trained one that grasps with a 9% scrabble rate baked in.

A git analogy: plain BC is like building your release by merging every commit in the history with equal trust, including the ones later reverted. AWR, which we are about to derive, weights each commit by whether the release it shipped in passed its tests. Where the analogy breaks down: commits are independent and a merge is binary, but robot actions are sequential and correlated — one bad action changes every state you see afterwards, so "blame" spreads across a whole episode rather than sitting on one line. Advantage estimation (Chapter 3) exists to handle that spreading, and reward shaping (Chapter 11) to sharpen it.

4.3.3 What a fix has to preserve

BC has a second, separate problem: compounding error under covariate shift, where small deviations take the policy to states the demonstrator never visited and errors snowball. That thread is picked up in Chapter 13 (DAgger, HG-DAgger, HIL-SERL). Set it aside for now.

So here is the question that defines the rest of the chapter. Can we keep the supervised loss — with all of its stability and architecture-independence — but make the data's quality matter?

4.4 AWR derived in slow motion

This is the longest derivation in Parts I and II, and it is the one everything after it stands on, so we take it at walking pace. Here is the map. There are three moves. First, take the data's own action distribution and tilt it toward the actions that turned out well, while keeping it on a leash — a limit on how far from the data it may move. The tilt follows a rule we derive rather than guess. The rule has one knob, the temperature \(\beta\); 4.4.3 shows where it comes from. Second, fit the network to that tilted distribution. Third, notice that the two moves together collapse into something almost embarrassingly simple: plain behavior cloning with one extra number attached to each logged sample. Figure 4.1 is that map as a picture.

Two promises about how this section is written. First: almost nothing in it is new. Almost every step has a twin in Chapter 3 that you have already survived — the surrogate objective of 3.2.3, the trust region of 3.3.1, the KL recipe of 3.3.2, the importance-sampling line of 3.2.2 — and we name each twin as we reach it. The two genuinely new pieces are the Lagrangian, introduced patiently in 4.4.3, and the idea of fitting a network to a target distribution by KL, which 4.4.4 shows you have in fact been doing since 4.3 without the name. Second: one small problem is carried from 4.4.2 to the end — one state of one grasp on your SO-101, three hundred logged frames, three actions, three advantages — and every formula in the section gets evaluated on it with a calculator. If a formula stops making sense, put the toy's numbers in.

4.4.1 The obvious thing to try: throw the bad data away

The simplest idea that could work: throw the bad data away. Compute a return for each episode, keep only the best — the top 10% by return, say — and behavior-clone that. This is a real method (filtered BC, or top-\(k\)% BC) and a respectable baseline you should run at least once.

Try it on the 40-episode grasp dataset of 4.3.2. Suppose the return penalizes wasted time (a discount factor or a per-step cost both do). Then the twelve scrabbling episodes score lowest. Put the cut just above them and you keep the twenty-eight clean episodes — 70% of the pool here, not the 10% above; the right fraction depends on the pool. The baked-in 9% scrabble rate goes to zero. Notice, though, that you could only place that cut because 4.3.2 told you there were exactly twelve bad episodes. On a real pool nothing tells you, and the cut is a guess: the first complaint below. Filtered BC is crude in ways you can feel:

  • The threshold is arbitrary. Why 10%? At 5% you have too little data to fit a big network; at 25% you are cloning mediocrity again. Nothing in the problem tells you where to cut.
  • It is all-or-nothing. An episode just below the cut contributes nothing, even if it was nearly perfect and failed on one frame. An episode just above it counts in full, even if it succeeded by luck.
  • It cannot express degrees. An episode twice as good as another gets the same treatment: included, at the same volume.
  • It works at the wrong grain. Quality lives in frames, but the filter operates on episodes. Each of those twelve scrabbling grasps fumbled for three seconds and then recovered: it holds 60 bad frames and a few hundred good ones, and an episode-level cut keeps or discards them together.

What we want is the soft version: every sample stays, but each speaks with a volume proportional to how good it was. Notice the question that sentence hides. Proportional how? Linearly, so an action twice as good counts twice? Then what of a below-average action, whose advantage is negative — does it count negatively, pushing the network away as in Chapter 2's policy gradient, or a little but positively? There is a whole family of curves that turn "how good" into "how loud," and picking one by taste is a guess.

So we will not guess. We write down what we want as a constrained optimization problem, in the same shape as TRPO's in Section 3.3.1, and solve it; the curve falls out of the solution. To make that solution checkable rather than something to take on trust, the next subsection first sets up a problem small enough to solve on paper.

4.4.2 The constrained problem, on one state of one grasp

State the goal honestly, in words first. We want the policy with the highest expected advantage, subject to not straying far from the data. The second clause is the medicine of 4.2 written into the problem instead of bolted on afterward. Before formalizing either clause, meet the toy.

The SO-101's gripper is 3 cm above a cube and slightly to the left of it. Over many teleop sessions, exactly three different things were ever done from this position:

  • \(a_1\): close the gripper now. The fingers close on air beside the cube; the grasp misses.
  • \(a_2\): descend 1 cm. The offset is still there; sometimes the grasp lands, sometimes not. Average.
  • \(a_3\): shift right 1 cm, then descend. The gripper centers on the cube and the grasp is clean.

Attach an advantage to each: \(\hat{A}(a_1) = -1\), \(\hat{A}(a_2) = 0\), \(\hat{A}(a_3) = +2\). As in Chapter 3, an advantage says how much better than usual an action turned out, judged against what typically happened from this state: \(a_2\) came out level with the baseline \(V(s)\) — the value each estimate is measured against — \(a_1\) one unit below it, \(a_3\) two units above. They are estimates, made with Chapter 3's tools, which is why they wear hats.

Now the data. Three hundred logged frames sit at this state, one hundred of each action. So the behavior policy at this state, the distribution the data itself follows, is

\[ \pi_\beta(a_1 \mid s) = \pi_\beta(a_2 \mid s) = \pi_\beta(a_3 \mid s) = \tfrac{1}{3}. \]

Formalize the first clause on the toy. The new policy \(\pi\) is three unknown numbers, \(\pi(a_1), \pi(a_2), \pi(a_3)\), non-negative and summing to one. Its expected advantage is

\[ \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi}\big[\hat{A}(a)\big] \;=\; \pi(a_1)\cdot(-1) \;+\; \pi(a_2)\cdot 0 \;+\; \pi(a_3)\cdot 2. \]

Put the data's own distribution in and you get \(-\tfrac{1}{3} + 0 + \tfrac{2}{3} = +\tfrac{1}{3}\): the score of cloning the data exactly as it is, which is what plain BC does. (A true advantage would average to zero over the data's own actions; ours average to \(+\tfrac{1}{3}\) because they are estimates against an imperfect baseline. This does not matter, and 4.4.3 shows why in one sentence.)

The obvious way to push this up is to put all the mass on \(a_3\): \(\pi = (0, 0, 1)\) scores \(2\), the maximum possible. That is filtered BC in its purest form, and there are two reasons not to trust it. The first is noise: the \(+2\) is an estimate from one hundred frames, and betting the whole policy on it is betting the run on one number.

The second is worse. The unconstrained problem puts all its mass on whichever action has the largest advantage, and nothing says that action was ever logged. Give the toy a fourth action \(a_4\), the \(+60^\circ\) wrist flex from 4.2, which no one ever performed. No logged return can score \(a_4\), because it was never taken; the only thing that can put a number on it is a critic asked to extrapolate, which is exactly what happened in 4.2. A critic asked about \(a_4\) will answer, and, as in 4.2, the answer is whatever flattering number its surface happens to hold out there; on the toy's scale call it \(+8\) — for an action that exists only in the critic's imagination. With nothing but the first clause, the answer is: always do the \(+60^\circ\) flex. We need the second clause.

Before writing it, notice that the first clause is not new to you. In Section 3.2.3 you maximized the surrogate \(L(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t[\rho_t(\theta)\,\hat{A}_t]\), and the one-line algebra of 3.2.2 showed that, with \(\rho\) the importance ratio \(\pi_\theta/\pi_{\theta_{old}}\), \(\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_{\theta_{old}}}[\rho\,\hat{A}] = \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_\theta}[\hat{A}]\): PPO's surrogate is, in words, the expected advantage of the old policy averaged over actions the new policy would choose. Our first clause is that sentence with \(\pi_{\theta_{old}}\) renamed \(\pi_\beta\). It tells the same lie 3.2.3 confessed to — it says nothing about the new policy later visiting different states — and, exactly as in Chapter 3, the lie grows with the distance from the policy that made the data. That is a third reason for a leash — noise and \(a_4\) were the first two — and it is the one Chapter 3 already gave you.

Now the second clause, and again you have seen it. TRPO in Section 3.3.1 took the honest route: since the surrogate is only trustworthy near the policy that generated the data, it constrained the KL divergence to that anchor policy to stay below a small threshold such as 0.01. Do the same thing here with two changes. The anchor is the behavior policy \(\pi_\beta\) rather than the previous version of the policy, \(\pi_{\theta_{old}}\), because \(\pi_\beta\) is who made the data. And the KL is written in the other direction — new policy on the left, data on the right; the paragraphs after the box explain why. Here the threshold is written \(\delta\):

\[ \max_{\pi} \; \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi(\cdot|s)}\!\left[ A^{\pi_\beta}(s,a) \right] \quad \text{s.t.} \quad D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left( \pi(\cdot|s) \,\|\, \pi_\beta(\cdot|s) \right) \le \delta . \]
In plain words

Read the left half first. \(\pi\) is the new policy we are solving for. \(\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi(\cdot|s)}[\cdot]\) means "sample an action from the new policy at state \(s\), and average." \(A^{\pi_\beta}(s,a)\) is the advantage of the behavior policy: how much better than average taking action \(a\) at \(s\) was, judged by what the data-generating policy went on to achieve; \(\hat{A}\) is our estimate of it. So the left half says: put the mass on above-average actions — on the toy, \(-\pi(a_1) + 2\pi(a_3)\). The right half is the leash. \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi \,\|\, \pi_\beta)\) measures how far the new distribution is from the data's, and \(\delta\) is how far we allow it: the radius of the leash, in nats, defined below. Small \(\delta\): tight leash, timid update. Large \(\delta\): loose leash, and the extrapolation disaster of 4.2 returns.

One letter to watch: this \(\delta\), with no subscript, is the leash radius, not the TD residual \(\delta_t\) of Chapter 3.

Read the KL the way Section 3.3.2 taught you: bind the two letters, then ask who is drawing the samples. In Chapter 3 you bound \(p\) to the old policy and \(q\) to the new one. Here \(p\) is the new policy \(\pi\) and \(q\) is the data's \(\pi_\beta\) — not TRPO's direction. The \(a_4\) check below shows what this direction buys, and 4.4.3 says in one paragraph what the other direction would have let through. The recipe still works: the new policy draws the action; for each action drawn, compare how likely the new policy was to take it against how often the data took it; average the log of that ratio.

That average is measured in nats: a nat is the unit of a KL whose logarithm is natural, as every \(\log\) in this chapter is. A KL of 1 nat means the log of the ratio averages to 1 over the actions the new policy takes. Undo the log and that says: a typical action is about \(e\), roughly 2.7, times more likely under the new policy than under the data. (Typical in the sense that it is the logarithm that is averaged, so some actions more, some less.) On the toy, with \(\pi_\beta = \tfrac{1}{3}\) everywhere,

\[ D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi \,\|\, \pi_\beta) \;=\; \sum_{a} \pi(a) \log \frac{\pi(a)}{\pi_\beta(a)} \;=\; \sum_a \pi(a) \log\big(3\,\pi(a)\big). \]

Two edge cases of the KL formula matter here. An action the new policy never takes contributes nothing: \(0 \cdot \log 0\) is read as 0. An action the data never took, given any positive probability by the new policy, contributes \(+\infty\): \(x \cdot \log(x/0)\) with \(x \gt 0\).

Put numbers in. At \(\pi = \pi_\beta\) every ratio is 1, every log is 0, and the KL is 0: the leash is slack. At the greedy policy — all mass on the single best-scoring action, \(\pi = (0, 0, 1)\) — the two actions it never takes contribute 0 and the only surviving term is \(1 \cdot \log 3 \approx 1.10\) nats. Now bring back \(a_4\). The data never took it, so \(\pi_\beta(a_4) = 0\). Give it any positive probability and its term is \(\pi(a_4)\log(\pi(a_4)/0) = +\infty\): the constraint cannot be satisfied at any \(\delta\). This direction of KL reports an infinite leash length for inventing an action the data never took — compare 3.3.2, where in the other direction such a move "barely registers directly." That is what will make AWR structurally safe offline.

One question is left hanging: who chooses \(\delta\)? In TRPO you set 0.01 by hand. Here, you will find, nobody does.

4.4.3 Solving it by hand: why the answer is an exponential

Here is the pleasant surprise. TRPO's version of this problem has no closed-form solution — no explicit formula, only an iteration — which is why Section 3.3.3 needed Fisher-vector products, conjugate gradients, and backtracking, and why Chapter 3 ended up with PPO's clip instead. This problem does have one. The difference: in TRPO the unknown is \(\theta\), millions of network weights, and the KL as a function of them is a curved surface you can only probe locally. Here the unknown is the distribution itself — on the toy, three numbers, with no network in the problem — which is what nonparametric means; and the answer is an explicit formula rather than something you iterate toward, which is what closed form means. That is why the derivation fits in a few lines. This step is where most readers get lost, so we take it slowly.

Six moves. Price the constraint (the Lagrangian). Differentiate one probability at a time. Solve, and watch the exponential appear. Put the toy in at two temperatures. Try three variants — unequal data, the unlogged action, and a different leash — the last of which is the real answer to "why an exponential." Finally, put numbers on what \(\beta\) buys in leash.

The tool is the Lagrangian, and here is all it means. You have a thing to maximize and a rule you must obey. Constrained problems are awkward because the best point may sit on the edge of the allowed region, where derivatives are not zero, so "set the derivative to zero" finds nothing there. Instead of obeying the rule, charge a price for breaking it: subtract from the objective a price per unit of leash used, then maximize the resulting unconstrained expression. The price is the Lagrange multiplier, and for the right price the priced problem and the constrained one have the same answer (the end of this subsection shows why, once we have numbers to do it with).

An analogy from work: a cloud budget. A hard cap says "this team may use at most \(\delta\) GPU-hours a month." A price says "each GPU-hour costs the team \(\beta\) dollars from its own budget." Under the price the team optimizes work minus cost, and for the right price it lands on exactly the usage the cap would have allowed; you steer usage by moving the price. Where the analogy breaks down: in the accounting version you fix the cap and search for the price that lands on it. AWR does the reverse: you fix the price \(\beta\), accept whatever leash length comes out, and never search for the \(\delta\) it corresponds to.
