\[ \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \gamma^t \big[\gamma\,\Phi(s_{t+1}) - \Phi(s_t)\big] \;=\; \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \big[\gamma^{t+1}\Phi(s_{t+1}) - \gamma^{t}\Phi(s_t)\big] \]

Write out the terms. The first bracket gives \(\gamma\Phi(s_1) - \Phi(s_0)\); the second gives \(\gamma^2\Phi(s_2) - \gamma\Phi(s_1)\), whose second half cancels the first bracket's first half. The same happens at every interior state: each \(\gamma^{t}\Phi(s_t)\) appears once positive and once negative. Everything in the middle collapses and only the ends survive, leaving \(\gamma^{T}\Phi(s_T) - \Phi(s_0)\).

Read what that means. The total shaping any trajectory can collect depends only on where it started and where it ended — not on the route, the length, or how many times it wobbled. The undiscounted potential difference around a closed loop is zero, which is why the pump is impossible. With \(\gamma\) slightly below 1 it is better than zero, from your point of view: a loop that leaves \(s_0\) and comes back after \(n\) steps collects \(\gamma^{n}\Phi(s_0) - \Phi(s_0) = \Phi(s_0)(\gamma^{n} - 1)\), which is a small net penalty whenever \(\Phi(s_0)\) is positive. Circling either pays nothing or costs you. It never pays.

An analogy from the physical world. \(\Phi\) is elevation and the shaping reward is gravitational potential energy: walk any route across a landscape and the net energy gained depends only on your start and end altitudes. Hikers cannot invent energy by walking in circles. Where it breaks down: gravity is exactly conservative, whereas \(\gamma\) tilts the field, and the cancellation above assumes \(\Phi(s_T) = 0\) at terminal states or that \(\gamma^T\) is negligible. Here it is not: \(0.999^{600} \approx 0.55\). The rigorous argument does not need that assumption — it is the uniform value shift \(V'(s) = V(s) - \Phi(s)\), which lowers every state's value equally and leaves every \(\arg\max\) untouched — but set \(\Phi\) to zero on terminal states anyway.

11.3.4 Choosing a potential

The ideal choice is \(\Phi \approx V^*\), the optimal value function — but if you had \(V^*\) you would not need any of this, so \(\Phi\) is a rough proxy in practice. Here is the theorem's real gift: a bad potential wastes your shaping budget and can slow learning, but it can never corrupt what "optimal" means. The worst case is wasted time, not a broken task. Very few knobs in RL have that property.

The practical \(\Phi\) in the LeHome solution is the completion head from Chapter 8: a linear probe on the policy's backbone, trained only on successful episodes to regress the elapsed fraction \(t/T\). Having seen nothing but successes, it encodes "what fraction of a good fold is done." Set \(\Phi(s) = \alpha_c \bar{C}(s)\) with \(\alpha_c = 0.5\), where \(\bar{C}\) is the smoothed head output.

That word "smoothed" hides a snag, and it is worth naming rather than stepping over. \(\bar{C}\) is an exponential moving average of the head's per-frame predictions (Section 11.4.2), so it is formally a function of the frame's history, not of \(s\) alone — and the theorem you just proved was about a \(\Phi\) that reads the state and nothing else. Applied literally, the chapter's own test rejects the chapter's own potential. There are two honest ways to close the gap. The clean one is to fold the smoother's running value into the state definition: it is one more number your pipeline already carries per frame, and once it is part of \(s\) the potential is state-only again by construction. The practical one is to notice that at coefficient 0.2 the smoothed value trails the raw head by a fraction of a single step's change, which is tiny next to the shaping magnitude \(\alpha_c = 0.5\) — so the invariance holds to a good approximation, and the residue is far below the noise you are fighting. Either answer is fine. Silently ignoring the question is not.

This channel earns its keep on saturated tasks. Once shorts fold at 93%, \(\hat{p}_{succ}\) is pinned near 1 and checkpoint rewards almost always pay, so the advantages of Sections 11.4 and 11.5 collapse toward zero and learning stalls. The completion potential still separates fast, clean progress from dawdling, so a gradient survives — and being potential-based, it runs at full strength in Section 11.6's blend.

Be precise about what "full strength, no risk" buys you, because it is a narrower claim than it sounds. The theorem says the shaping cannot change which policy is optimal in the MDP. It does not say the machinery downstream of \(\hat{A}\) is unaffected. Chapter 4 feeds \(\hat{A}\) through \(\exp(\hat{A}_i/\beta)\) and Chapter 10 through a threshold, both nonlinear, and at any finite \(\beta\) adding a shaping term genuinely moves sampling priorities and conditioning labels around. That is the whole reason you added it. So read the guarantee as "no risk of redefining the task," not "no effect" — the shaping changes what your optimizer looks at first, which is exactly what you wanted, while leaving the definition of success untouched, which is what you were afraid of losing.

Pitfalls
A raw progress bonus — "+k whenever the cuff gets closer" — is not potential-based, because it depends on the transition rather than a fixed function of state, and it is exploitable exactly as the bicycle was. Section 11.2.2's running-min rule patches one instance; it is no general defense. The test: can you write your bonus as \(\gamma\Phi(s') - \Phi(s)\) for a \(\Phi\) that reads only the current state? If not, assume it changes the optimal policy.

11.4 The value function for free

11.4.1 The obvious cost, and how to avoid it

GAE (Chapter 3) needs a value estimate \(V(s)\) at every frame. The standard answer is a critic network: a second head, a second loss, a second set of hyperparameters, and a real slice of your compute. On rl-rover that was free — the critic was a three-layer MLP. On a Gemma-2B backbone it is not.

You do not have to pay it. Chapter 8 already put a success head on the model: a linear probe on the policy's backbone, trained with cross-entropy against the eventual outcome, outputting \(\hat{p}_{succ}(s)\), the predicted probability that this episode ends in success given the current frame. It is already a value function, up to one bookkeeping term.

\[ V(s_t) \;=\; \hat{p}_{succ}(s_t) \;-\; R_{acc,t}, \qquad R_{acc,t} \;=\; \sum_{k \lt t} r_k \]
In plain words
The left side is the value of the current state — the total reward you expect from here to the end. \(\hat{p}_{succ}(s_t)\) is the success head's output at this frame, between 0 and 1. \(R_{acc,t}\) is the accumulated reward: the sum of every reward already paid strictly before the current step, which under the checkpoint scheme is 0, or 0.5, or something in between. The \(t\) in the subscript is doing real work — this quantity changes as the episode runs, growing by \(r_t\) at every step, so it must be read at the same frame as \(V(s_t)\). This chapter keeps that subscript because the timestep is the point here; elsewhere in the book, where only one frame is under discussion, the same quantity is written \(R_{acc}\). So: your expected future reward is your probability of eventually succeeding, minus whatever the episode already paid you. The subtraction is there because the total is capped at 1 — if half the credit is banked, only half remains to collect.

11.4.2 Verify it yourself, by cases

Worth checking rather than believing. Set \(\gamma \approx 1\) and enumerate the two possible futures. If the episode succeeds, the scheme tops the cumulative total up to exactly 1.0 at the success frame; it has already paid \(R_{acc,t}\), so the rewards still to come sum to \(1 - R_{acc,t}\). If it fails, withdrawal claws back everything granted, so the episode total is 0 and what remains sums to \(-R_{acc,t}\). Those are the only outcomes, and the head gives their probabilities:

\[ \mathbb{E}[G_t \mid s_t] = \hat{p}_{succ}\,(1 - R_{acc,t}) + (1 - \hat{p}_{succ})\,(-R_{acc,t}) = \hat{p}_{succ} - \hat{p}_{succ}R_{acc,t} - R_{acc,t} + \hat{p}_{succ}R_{acc,t} = \hat{p}_{succ} - R_{acc,t} \]

The two \(\hat{p}_{succ}R_{acc,t}\) terms cancel and the claim falls out. Note what \(R_{acc,t}\) is not: not learned, not predicted, carrying no error. It is a running sum known exactly. All the uncertainty lives in \(\hat{p}_{succ}\), which is the honest place for it. From \(V\) you get \(\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)\) and then \(\hat{A}_t\) with Chapter 3's GAE machinery — LeHome uses \(\gamma = 0.999\), \(\lambda = 0.99\), computed offline over all stored rollouts before each iteration.

Two practical touches appear in no equation. Smooth \(\hat{p}_{succ}\) with an exponential moving average (coefficient 0.2), because per-frame probe predictions jitter and jittery GAE differences are advantage noise. And interpolate the last thirty frames toward the known outcome: on a stored episode you already hold the answer, so do not let a noisy head disagree with it.

11.5 The damped baseline

11.5.1 Chapter 2's promise, and its fine print

Chapter 2 taught that subtracting a baseline \(V(s)\) from the return leaves the policy gradient unbiased and reduces its variance. True. The fine print: reduces is guaranteed only for a good baseline. A wrong value estimate can add variance instead — and in the pipelines of Chapters 4 and 10, where \(\hat{A}\) passes through \(\exp(\hat{A}_i/\beta)\), clipping, and sampling priorities, it adds bias too, because those transformations are nonlinear in \(\hat{A}\). Your value head is a linear probe trained on a moving target. It is decent. It is not good.

11.5.2 The A/B testing view

The cleanest way to see what to do comes from online experimentation. In case you have never run an experiment platform: you want to know whether a new checkout page raises revenue per user, so you split users into two arms and compare mean revenue. Spending varies enormously — most users spend nothing, one spends four thousand dollars — so the effect is buried in noise. But you have a covariate: each user's spend before the experiment, which correlates with their spend during it and, fixed before randomization, cannot have been affected by the treatment. CUPED subtracts it (Deng et al., 2013). Instead of analyzing the outcome \(Y\) directly, you analyze \(Y - \theta(X - \bar{X})\), where \(X\) is the user's pre-experiment spend, \(\bar{X}\) is the average of \(X\) over everyone, and \(\theta\) is a fitted coefficient, not 1. Both details matter. The centering by \(\bar{X}\) is what keeps the adjusted quantity an unbiased estimate of \(\mathbb{E}[Y]\), since the subtracted term has mean zero. The fitted \(\theta\) is what makes the variance actually drop.

A baseline is the same object: a control variate, a correlated quantity you subtract to cut variance without biasing the estimate you actually care about. Be careful about which estimate that is. In the A/B case it is the mean of \(Y\), which the centering protects. In the RL case it is the policy gradient, not the mean of the advantage — subtracting \(\alpha V\) does shift the average advantage by \(\alpha\mathbb{E}[V]\), and the gradient survives anyway, for a reason spelled out just below the equation. So subtract \(\alpha V\) rather than \(V\), with a damping coefficient \(\alpha\), and expand:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(G - \alpha V) = \operatorname{Var}(G) - 2\alpha \operatorname{Cov}(G, V) + \alpha^2 \operatorname{Var}(V), \qquad \alpha^* = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(G, V)}{\operatorname{Var}(V)} = \rho_{GV}\,\frac{\sigma_G}{\sigma_V} \]
In plain words
\(G\) is the return actually observed for a frame; \(V\) is what the value head predicted for it; \(\alpha\) is how much of that prediction you subtract. The left side is the variance of the resulting advantage estimate. On the right, \(\operatorname{Var}(G)\) is the noise you started with, \(\operatorname{Cov}(G,V)\) measures how much \(G\) and \(V\) move together, \(\operatorname{Var}(V)\) how much the prediction bounces. The middle term is the payoff, linear in \(\alpha\); the last is the cost, quadratic. That is an upward parabola with one minimum, found by setting the derivative to zero: \(\alpha^*\). Here \(\sigma_G, \sigma_V\) are the standard deviations of \(G\) and \(V\), and \(\rho_{GV}\) their correlation — unrelated to Chapter 3's ratio \(\rho_t(\theta)\), hence the subscript.

Settle one worry before going further, because otherwise it will nag at you for the rest of the chapter. Section 11.5.1 opened by promising that subtracting a baseline leaves the policy gradient unbiased. Does scaling that baseline by \(\alpha = 0.5\) break the promise? No, and the reason is worth seeing once. The unbiasedness argument never needed the subtracted quantity to be the right value function. It only needed it to be a function of the state and not of the action, because then

\[ \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_\theta}\big[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a|s)\, b(s)\big] \;=\; b(s)\,\nabla_\theta \sum_a \pi_\theta(a|s) \;=\; b(s)\,\nabla_\theta 1 \;=\; 0 \]

for any such \(b\). And \(\alpha V(s)\) is a function of the state alone for every constant \(\alpha\) — scaling a state-only quantity leaves it state-only. So \(\alpha\) is a pure variance knob. It cannot tilt the gradient, whatever value you give it, including 0 and including 5. What it does change is the variance, which is the whole point, and the average size of \(\hat{A}\), which matters only where something nonlinear reads it. That is the one place bias does enter, and Section 11.5.1 already flagged it: \(\exp(\hat{A}_i/\beta)\) in Chapter 4 and the threshold in Chapter 10 respond to \(\hat{A}\) itself, not only to its expectation. The deliberate reward leak of Section 11.5.4 inherits exactly the same caveat — a variance-and-scale choice, not a broken gradient.

Substituting \(\alpha^*\) back gives the minimum achievable variance, \(\operatorname{Var}(G)(1 - \rho_{GV}^2)\). Read the formulas against your situation. A perfect value function satisfies \(G = V + \text{noise}\), so \(\operatorname{Cov}(G,V) = \operatorname{Var}(V)\) and \(\alpha^* = 1\) — full subtraction, Chapter 2's textbook case. A noisy head inflates \(\sigma_V\) and shrinks \(\rho_{GV}\), and both push \(\alpha^*\) below 1. And whenever \(\sigma_V \gt 2\rho_{GV}\,\sigma_G\), full subtraction is worse than no baseline at all.

11.5.3 Worked example

Real numbers, and one sentence of setup so you know which frame we are standing on. Take a frame early in the episode, before any checkpoint has paid, so \(R_{acc,t} = 0\) and the return-to-go is exactly the binary outcome of Section 11.4: 1 if the episode eventually succeeds, 0 if it fails. Put the success probability at \(p = 0.5\), roughly where a mid-training garment sits. Then \(G\) is a coin flip and \(\operatorname{Var}(G) = p(1-p)\). Frames later in the episode, after a checkpoint has banked 0.5, have a return-to-go of \(1 - R_{acc,t}\) or \(-R_{acc,t}\) and a correspondingly smaller spread; the arithmetic below is the clean early-frame case, which is also the worst case for variance.

One number in what follows deserves a raised eyebrow before you read past it: \(\sigma_V = 0.7\) is larger than \(\sigma_G = 0.5\). That says the value head's predictions bounce around more than the returns they are predicting. A well-calibrated predictor of a binary outcome cannot do that, because its output is a conditional mean and averaging never adds spread — calibration forces \(\sigma_V \le \sigma_G\). So \(\sigma_V \gt \sigma_G\) is not an incidental choice of numbers; it is itself the diagnostic that the head is miscalibrated or badly scaled. That is precisely the regime this section exists for, which is why the numbers stay as they are.

Var(G) = p(1 - p) = 0.5 x 0.5              = 0.25
sigma_G = sqrt(0.25)                       = 0.5

Your value head is noisy:
sigma_V = 0.7   ->  Var(V) = 0.7 x 0.7     = 0.49
rho_GV  = 0.6
Cov(G,V) = rho_GV x sigma_G x sigma_V
         = 0.6 x 0.5 x 0.7                 = 0.21

Full subtraction, alpha = 1:
  Var = 0.25 - 2(1)(0.21) + (1)(0.49)
      = 0.25 - 0.42 + 0.49                 = 0.32
  vs no baseline (0.25):  0.32 / 0.25      = 1.28   -> +28% variance

Optimal damping:
  alpha* = Cov / Var(V) = 0.21 / 0.49      = 0.4286
  check:  rho x sigma_G / sigma_V = 0.6 x 0.5 / 0.7 = 0.4286  (agrees)
  Var = 0.25 - 2(0.4286)(0.21) + (0.4286)^2 (0.49)
      = 0.25 - 0.18 + 0.09                 = 0.16
  formula: Var(G)(1 - rho^2) = 0.25 x (1 - 0.36) = 0.16       (agrees)
  vs no baseline:  0.16 / 0.25 = 0.64      -> -36% variance

So the textbook move makes things 28% worse here, and the correctly scaled move 36% better. The gap is one coefficient. The "worse than nothing" condition is visible directly: \(\sigma_V = 0.7\) while \(2\rho_{GV}\sigma_G = 0.6\). Figure 11.2 plots the parabola.

11.5.4 The second, deliberate effect of damping

Damping does something else that is easy to miss, and it is intentional. With \(V(s_t) = \alpha(\hat{p}_{succ,t} - R_{acc,t})\), substitute into the TD residual:

\[ \delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t) \;\approx\; (1 - \alpha\gamma)\,r_t \;+\; \alpha\big(\gamma\,\hat{p}_{succ,t+1} - \hat{p}_{succ,t}\big) \]

The algebra is short: \(R_{acc,t+1} = R_{acc,t} + r_t\) by definition, so those terms almost cancel, leaving a residue \(\alpha R_{acc,t}(1-\gamma)\) negligible at \(\gamma = 0.999\) — hence "approximately." Now read the first term. An undamped, accurate baseline makes \((1 - \alpha\gamma) \approx 0\), cancelling checkpoint rewards almost entirely. That is technically correct — the head saw the checkpoint coming, so it was priced in — but it means the dense signal of Section 11.2 is subtracted away by the estimator meant to use it. Damping at \(\alpha = 0.5\) leaves \((1 - 0.5 \times 0.999) \approx 0.5\), so half of every checkpoint reward passes through as raw signal, deliberately left un-explained.

In the LeHome solution
Larchenko damped with \(\alpha_s = 0.5\) — his name for this section's \(\alpha\), subscripted for the success channel to keep it apart from the completion-shaping \(\alpha_c\) of Section 11.3.4 — chosen by instinct rather than derivation. The paper's v2 works out \(\alpha^* = \rho_{GV}\,\sigma_G/\sigma_V\) and measures it from logged rollouts: the true per-garment optimum ranged roughly 0.4 to 0.8, median near 0.5. He calls it "a mistake that worked" (Larchenko, 2026). You can do better than luck — both \(V\) and \(G\) already sit in your rollout logs. Estimate \(\rho_{GV}\), \(\sigma_G\), \(\sigma_V\) from a few thousand frames per garment type, and set \(\alpha\) from the formula.

11.6 Stale values and the group anchor

11.6.1 A failure mode created by your own infrastructure

One more problem, born entirely of Chapter 14's asynchronous loop. Two details matter there. Value predictions \(\hat{p}_{succ}\) are recorded at collection time and never recomputed — re-running the backbone over millions of stored frames every iteration would cost more than training. And old rollout datasets are not deleted; their sampling share decays slowly, so they linger for many iterations. A large fraction of your training data therefore carries value estimates made by a policy several generations old.

This is stale off-policy data, and staleness is worse than noise. Noise averages out over a batch; a stale head is systematically wrong in one direction, misjudging exactly the states where the policy has recently improved — the regime Section 11.5 warned about.

Think of it as a cached computed column that nobody invalidates. The difference is that a database can detect staleness by comparing cache to source; here, checking a stored prediction means recomputing it, the expense you were avoiding. You cannot fix this by detecting it. You have to build an estimator that does not care.

11.6.2 An advantage with no value function in it

GRPO — Group Relative Policy Optimization (Shao et al., 2024) — does exactly that for language models. For a given prompt it samples a group of responses from the same policy, scores them all, and sets each response's advantage to its own reward minus the group mean, divided by the group standard deviation. The group mean is the baseline. No critic is trained, and none can drift, because the baseline is recomputed from fresh samples every time.

The robotics translation swaps "prompt" for "task instance." Group episodes by garment, the closest thing to the same prompt. Split each episode into two segments at the first checkpoint: everything strictly before the frame where the checkpoint paid, and that frame onward. A segment is then a coarse unit of behavior, and each segment is scored against its own baseline.

The two baselines are different quantities, which is the part worth stating explicitly. Segment one is scored against the garment's empirical checkpoint rate — the fraction of recent episodes on that garment that reached the checkpoint at all. Reaching it scores \(1 - \text{rate}\); missing it scores \(-\text{rate}\). Segment two is scored against the empirical success rate given the checkpoint, \(P(\text{success} \mid \text{checkpoint})\), because once the checkpoint is banked that conditional is what "typical" means for the rest of the episode. An episode that never reaches the checkpoint has no second segment: it is one segment, the whole episode, scored against the checkpoint rate. All these rates are plain counts over recent rollouts, recomputed every iteration, then scaled to match GAE magnitudes so the channels can be added — the scale factor is the segment's mean discount weight, \((1 - \gamma^{n})/(n(1-\gamma))\) for a segment of \(n\) frames, which is what one unit of outcome would be worth after GAE had spread it over those frames. Nothing here is learned, so nothing goes stale. The price is resolution: one number per segment, no per-step credit.

11.6.3 Blending by freshness

Two channels with complementary weaknesses: GAE is fine-grained but leans on an aging value head; the group anchor is coarse but ageless. Blend them by data age, and add Section 11.3's shaping on top as a third channel. Give the shaping its own per-step reward \(F_t = \gamma\Phi(s_{t+1}) - \Phi(s_t)\) and run that through the same GAE recursion the reward channel uses, so all three terms arrive on the same footing and can simply be added:

\[ \tilde{A}_t \;=\; \underbrace{w\,\hat{A}^{\mathrm{GAE}}_t}_{\substack{\text{per-step credit,}\\ \text{fades as data ages}}} \;+\; \underbrace{(1 - w)\,\hat{A}^{\mathrm{grp}}_t}_{\substack{\text{group outcome anchor,}\\ \text{stale-proof}}} \;+\; \underbrace{\hat{A}^{\Phi}_t}_{\substack{\text{potential shaping,}\\ \text{always full strength}}} \]
In plain words
\(\tilde{A}_t\) is the final advantage for frame \(t\), the number everything downstream consumes. The first term is Section 11.4's GAE estimate, which knows about individual timesteps but trusts the value head. The second is the group-relative estimate, which knows only "this segment did better or worse than typical for this garment" but trusts nothing that can age. The weight \(w\), between 0 and 1, decides which you lean on. It is tied to the dataset's sampling share — the fraction of each training batch drawn from that dataset, which decays as the dataset ages (Chapter 14). Fresh data gets \(w\) near 1 and uses fine-grained credit; decayed data gets \(w\) near 0 and degrades into outcome-only anchoring rather than trusting an obsolete prediction. This \(w\) is a data-freshness weight and has nothing to do with the AWR weight \(w_i = \exp(\hat{A}_i/\beta)\) of Chapter 4. \(\hat{A}^{\Phi}_t\) is the shaping channel just described: the per-step bonus \(F_t = \gamma\Phi(s_{t+1}) - \Phi(s_t)\) pushed through that same GAE recursion. It carries no weight of its own because, as Section 11.3.4 argued, it cannot change which policy is optimal — though it does move what the sampler looks at, which is why you added it.

Finally, normalize \(\tilde{A}\) by a global standard deviation measured on unbiased rollouts — the episodes collected by plain random or curriculum selection, the ones that alone count toward your success statistics, as opposed to the replay and hard-mining rollouts that deliberately oversample particular states (Chapter 14) — and clip to \([-2, 2]\) before it feeds Chapter 4's AWR sampler and Chapter 10's conditioning token. LeHome adds a garnish: the tightest 20% of successes per garment, ranked by the worst per-condition margin at the final frame, get \(+0.3\) on every frame, nudging the policy from barely-passing folds toward comfortable ones. Figure 11.3 lays out the finished pipeline end to end.

11.6.4 Second worked example: one frame, all three terms

Take the checkpoint frame of a long-sleeved-top episode that eventually succeeded, so \(r_t = 0.5\), with \(\alpha = 0.5\), \(\gamma = 0.999\), smoothed heads \(\hat{p}_{succ,t} = 0.55\) and \(\hat{p}_{succ,t+1} = 0.62\), and \(R_{acc,t} = 0\) because nothing has paid out yet. Say the checkpoint lands at step 200 of a 600-step episode, so the second segment runs for the remaining \(n = 400\) frames — that number is needed for the group anchor's scale factor.

V(s_t)   = 0.5 x (0.55 - 0.00)          = 0.275
V(s_t+1) = 0.5 x (0.62 - 0.50)          = 0.060     # R_acc,t+1 is now 0.5
delta_t  = 0.5 + 0.999 x 0.060 - 0.275  = 0.28494
cross-check with 11.5.4's shortcut:
  (1 - alpha x gamma) x r_t = 0.5005 x 0.5          = 0.25025
  alpha x (gamma x p_t+1 - p_t) = 0.5 x 0.06938     = 0.03469
  sum                                               = 0.28494  (agrees)

Suppose GAE accumulates this and later residuals to A_GAE = 0.42.
Group anchor: post-checkpoint segment succeeded -> score 1
  empirical P(success | checkpoint) for this garment = 0.62
  raw = 1 - 0.62                                     = 0.38
  scale = mean discount weight over the n = 400 frames of the segment
        = (1 - 0.999^400) / (400 x 0.001) = 0.32982 / 0.4  = 0.8246
  A_grp = 0.38 x 0.8246                              = 0.3133
Shaping: completion head rose 0.31 -> 0.44, so F_t = gamma x Phi' - Phi
  A_phi = 0.5 x (0.999 x 0.44 - 0.31) = 0.5 x 0.12956 = 0.06478
Freshness: data 25 iterations old, decay 0.98/iter
  w = 0.98^25                                        = 0.60
Blend = 0.60 x 0.42 + 0.40 x 0.3133 + 0.06478        = 0.4421
Normalize by global std 0.35: 0.4421 / 0.35          = 1.26
Tightest 20% of successes, so +0.3                   = 1.56 (inside clip)

Trace what each number did. Of the 0.285 residual, 0.250 is raw reward leaking through — exactly the \((1-\alpha\gamma)\) fraction. GAE then contributed the largest share of the blend, 0.252, because this data is only moderately aged; the group anchor contributed 0.125, and more if the data were older; shaping contributed 0.065, small but never zero, which keeps a gradient alive where the other two collapse. Normalization turned an unreadable 0.442 into a 1.26 that means something fixed: about 1.3 standard deviations better than average.

Two lines in that block deserve a note, because both are places where a reader is entitled to ask "where did that come from." The scale factor 0.8246 is not a magic constant: it is the mean discount weight \((1-\gamma^{n})/(n(1-\gamma))\) over the segment, from Section 11.6.2, and it is the only quantity in the example that depends on how long the segment is. Recompute it for your own horizon rather than copying the number — at \(n = 600\) it would be 0.75, at \(n = 900\) it would be 0.66. And the shaping line shows this frame's own \(F_t\) rather than the full GAE of the shaping channel; running the recursion would fold in later frames as well, but the single step is the piece you can check by hand, and it is the piece that carries the \(\gamma\) most people quietly drop.

Pitfalls
Advantage scale drift across task groups. \(\hat{A}\) enters \(\exp(\hat{A}/\beta)\) in Chapter 4 and a threshold in Chapter 10, so its scale silently acts as a temperature. A near-saturated garment may produce advantages of \(\pm 0.1\) while a struggling one swings \(\pm 0.8\). Blend those unnormalized and the struggling type dominates sampler and gradient alike — which sounds desirable until you notice it also dominates when its advantages are pure noise. Use one global normalizer plus clipping, and re-check per-group standard deviations whenever a group saturates.
Words you will hear
Dense vs sparse reward — dense pays out most timesteps, sparse only at the end; "sparse-reward task" is shorthand for "hard exploration problem." Reward hacking — the policy scores well on your reward function while failing the task you meant. Potential function \(\Phi\) — a state-only score used to build provably safe shaping. Control variate — a correlated quantity subtracted to cut an estimator's variance without biasing the thing you actually want to estimate; a baseline is one. Stale off-policy data — samples, or predictions stored with them, produced by an older policy than the one being trained. Group-relative — advantage computed by comparing samples of the same task instance instead of against a learned critic.
Checkpoint
  • Explain why a 600-step task with one terminal bit yields a zero gradient, naming the sparsity and horizon-variance failures separately.
  • Describe the two exploits checkpoint rewards invite — cyclic farming and bank-then-thrash — say which mechanism blocks each, and state precisely what reward withdrawal preserves and what it changes.
  • State the potential-shaping theorem, sketch the telescoping argument, and explain why a bad \(\Phi\) wastes effort but cannot change the optimal policy.
  • Derive \(V(s_t) = \hat{p}_{succ}(s_t) - R_{acc,t}\) by cases, and say why \(R_{acc,t}\) contributes no estimation error.
  • Compute \(\alpha^*\) from \(\rho_{GV}\), \(\sigma_G\), \(\sigma_V\), show that \(\alpha = 1\) can be worse than no baseline, and explain why scaling the baseline is a variance choice that leaves the policy gradient unbiased.
  • Explain why asynchronous training makes stored value predictions stale, and how a group anchor computed from empirical rates sidesteps that.

Where to go deeper. Ng, Harada, and Russell (1999) is short and worth reading in full — the necessity direction, the claim that only potential-based shaping is safe, is the surprising half most papers skip. Deng et al. (2013) introduces CUPED, the fastest way to internalize control variates. Schulman et al. (2016) covers the GAE machinery this chapter reuses, and Shao et al. (2024) presents GRPO where the group structure is far more obvious than in robotics. Sections 5 and 6 of Larchenko (2026) show every idea here deployed together; Appendix A gives links and a reading order.

Chapter 12 — Inference-time optimization

Every chapter so far has changed the policy's weights, at a cost of GPU-days: Chapter 10 changed what the network is told about each sample, Chapter 11 the numbers the critic hands it. This chapter freezes the checkpoint — not one gradient step, not one new episode of data — and moves the measured success rate by changing only how it is executed. In LeHome those choices mattered enough that Larchenko built an online tuning system for them (Larchenko, 2026).

The reason this is possible: a generative chunk policy is not a controller. A controller is a function from observation to action; once you have it there is nothing left to decide. A chunk policy is a sampler, and a sampler leaves unfinished business. How many of the \(H\) predicted actions do you execute before asking again? At what speed? What happens at the seam between chunks? How hard do you push the advantage condition from Chapter 10? None of these has an answer inside the weights. Every one of them moves the number.

12.1 Free success rate

Make it concrete. Your policy is Chapter 8's: a vision-language-action model whose action expert emits a chunk \(a_{t:t+H}\) by integrating a learned velocity field. In LeHome, \(H = 30\) twelve-dimensional joint-delta actions — one second at 30 Hz — from \(K = 10\) Euler steps of the flow ODE of Chapter 7.

Training fixed the distribution chunks are drawn from. It did not fix what you do with one. That gap splits into three families. One: how much of a chunk you run and how fast (Section 12.2). Two: how consecutive chunks are stitched, since each is generated from a stale observation while the arm is moving (Section 12.3). Three: how the chunk is drawn at all — how hard to push the advantage condition, how wide the noise you start from is, one candidate or several (Sections 12.4 and 12.5). Seven decisions, each tuned per garment type in LeHome, and Section 12.6 tunes all seven without a grid search.

One framing note. In classical deep RL there is essentially no inference-time surface: your PPO rover policy emits a Gaussian, you take the mean, you are done. A flow policy has an entire iterative sampling procedure between observation and action, all of it adjustable after training. That is new surface area, and it is easy to leave free success rate on the table because your previous tools never had any.

Words you will hear
Inference-time compute — work spent per decision at deployment (extra sampler steps, extra candidates) rather than in training; "scaling" it means buying accuracy with latency. Guidance scale — the multiplier \(g\) on a conditional-minus-unconditional difference; papers also write \(w\), \(s\), or \(\alpha\). Temperature — a scale on sampling noise; low means more deterministic, less diverse samples. Arm — one option a bandit can choose. Posterior — your belief about a quantity, as a distribution, after seeing data. Verifier — any model that scores a candidate output; in LLM work, "best-of-N with a verifier."

12.2 Execution length, playback speed, and chunk switching

12.2.1 How much of the chunk to execute

What we want is closed-loop control: the robot should notice when the world stops matching its plan, quickly.

The obvious thing is to execute the chunk: all thirty actions, then ask for the next second. One expensive forward pass buys a full second of seamless behavior.

Here is exactly how it fails. Your arm is 400 ms into a one-second reach toward a sleeve when the gripper brushes the fabric and the sleeve slides two centimeters left. The remaining 600 ms were computed from an observation in which the sleeve was elsewhere, and the policy will not be asked again until they are done — so the arm closes its fingers on empty table. The judgment was not wrong; it was stale. You have built an open-loop controller and called it closed-loop.

The fix is receding-horizon execution: run only the first \(n_e \le H\) actions, discard the rest, re-query from a fresh observation. With \(n_e = 5\) at 30 Hz the policy re-plans every 167 ms — boundaries at ticks 0, 5, 10, 15 — and the sleeve slid at 400 ms, which is tick 12. So it is noticed at the next boundary, tick 15: 100 ms and three control ticks later, instead of eighteen. Notice why the chunk was worth predicting anyway: predicting a full second forces the network to commit to a coherent intention rather than a twitchy per-step average. You keep the coherence and discard the staleness.

You do pay. Smaller \(n_e\) means more chunk boundaries, each a potential discontinuity — Section 12.3 exists because of this — more forward passes per second, and less within-chunk smoothness reaching the motors. Larchenko's tuned values were 3 to 5 out of 30: six to ten re-plans per second of predicted motion.

On your rig
LeRobot exposes this knob directly and most people never touch it: for an ACT or pi0-style policy on your SO-101, n_action_steps versus chunk_size is exactly \(n_e\) versus \(H\). Sweep it before retraining anything — 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 against a fixed checkpoint, twenty trials each. You will usually find a clear interior optimum, for an afternoon's work instead of a week's. On rl-rover, action repeat and control rate trade reactivity against smoothness the same way. You also already own the verifier of Section 12.5: your HIL-SERL SAC critic. Sample a handful of chunks, score each with the min over the critic ensemble, execute the argmax — and validate against random choice before trusting it, per the pitfall box.

12.2.2 Playback speed

A chunk is a time-indexed trajectory: action 0 is meant for now, action 1 for 33 ms from now. Nothing forces you to honor that timing — you can resample it onto a different number of control ticks. Larchenko's BEHAVIOR-1K entry (Larchenko et al., 2025) resampled 26 predicted actions with cubic splines onto 20 control ticks: 26 ticks of motion become 20, so the same path is replayed 26/20 = 1.3 times faster and takes 20/26 = 77% as long. Keep those two numbers apart, because it is easy to quote the wrong one: a 1.3x speed increase is a 23% cut in cycle time, not a 30% cut. Speed up and time saved are not the same quantity, and the difference grows as the ratio does. So: 23% less time on the clock for zero training and no new data.

But speed is not uniformly safe, and the interesting part is the exception rule: compression was disabled whenever the gripper state changed significantly. Reaching through free space tolerates being rushed. Closing fingers on a garment does not — a grasp replayed at 1.3x gives the fabric and the contact forces 23% less time to settle. So the policy sprints between contacts and walks through them. In LeHome this knob is a per-garment-type playback stretch.

12.2.3 Chunk switching

The third decision: when a new chunk arrives while the old one is still running, how much should the old constrain the new? Larchenko parameterizes this with an anchor length \(n_a\) — how many of the new chunk's actions are pulled toward the old chunk rather than generated freely, tuned small, 3 to 6 out of 30. Note the word "pulled." This is a soft influence, a weight that fades to nothing across those few slots, not a rule the new chunk has to obey. There is also a hard part, where some actions are copied over exactly and are not negotiable at all, and the two are separate knobs. Both, and the reason a generative model can be made to honor either, are the next section.

12.3 Action-chunk inpainting: executing while you think

12.3.1 The problem is latency, and the arm does not stop

A VLA forward pass is not free: the vision backbone and the language transformer run over three camera images before the action expert takes one step, costing tens to hundreds of milliseconds. Meanwhile the robot has momentum and will not hover in mid-air while you think. The obvious first attempt is synchronous execution — run the chunk, stop, think, run the next. You see it in demo videos once you know to look: the arm moves, freezes for a beat, moves again. For quasi-static tasks that is merely ugly; with dynamics it is a failure mode, because the world moves during the pause.

So you go asynchronous, the instinct of anyone who has prefetched anything: start generating chunk \(k{+}1\) while chunk \(k\) executes, and swap when it is ready.

Here is how that fails. Suppose generation takes 235 ms and your control period is 33 ms. By then the arm has executed seven or eight more actions from chunk \(k\)'s tail — but chunk \(k{+}1\) was generated from the observation of 235 ms ago and begins with its own idea of what those actions should have been. The two do not match: chunk \(k\) drifted left, chunk \(k{+}1\) assumes nothing moved. Swap them and the commanded position jumps. With a delta-action policy — LeHome's are joint deltas — that is worse than aesthetic: a delta is added to the current state, so you apply a correction meant for a configuration the arm has already left. The result is a violent jerk at every boundary, six to ten times a second.

12.3.2 The fix: freeze what is committed, blend the seam, generate the rest

Real-time chunking (Black et al., 2025) fixes this by noticing that some of the disagreement is not disagreement at all — it is already history.

By the time chunk \(k{+}1\) is ready, the first \(n_f\) of its actions have already been executed, from chunk \(k\)'s tail. They are not up for discussion; the arm is where it is. So freeze them: constrain the new chunk's first \(n_f\) actions to equal the committed tail exactly. Pull the next few softly toward the old chunk with a weight decaying to zero — the anchor region of length \(n_a\), which makes the seam smooth rather than merely continuous. The rest is generated freely (Figure 12.1). The name comes from image editing: inpainting is filling a masked-out region consistently with the rest of the picture — here, the chunk's future given the prefix that already ran.

An analogy from your day job. This is speculative execution with a commit point. A CPU predicts a branch and executes down the predicted path; when the real answer arrives, anything already retired is permanent and the rest can be revised. Real-time chunking gives the robot the same structure: retired actions frozen, in-flight actions blended, the not-yet-issued tail free. Where it breaks down: a CPU can squash a mispredicted path and lose only cycles. A robot cannot un-move. There is no rollback, which is why the frozen prefix must be respected exactly rather than merely preferred.

12.3.3 The mechanism: a correction to the velocity field

How do you force a flow model to respect a prefix? Overwriting the finished chunk's first \(n_f\) actions afterward does not work: the rest was generated without knowing about the overwrite and would not connect to it. The constraint has to be present during generation. Recall from Chapter 7: start from noise \(a^0 = z\) and integrate the velocity field \(v_\theta(a^u, u, o)\) forward in flow time \(u\) from 0 to 1 in \(K\) Euler steps. Inpainting adds a correction at each step:

\[ a^u_{0:n_f} \leftarrow a^{\mathrm{prev}}_{n_f':n_f'+n_f}, \qquad \tilde v_j(a^u,u,o) \;=\; v_{\theta,j}(a^u,u,o)\;+\;W_j\,\frac{a^{\mathrm{prev}}_{n_f'+j} - a^u_j}{1-u} \]
In plain words
The first line is the hard freeze: slots \(0\) through \(n_f-1\) of the chunk being generated, written \(a^u_{0:n_f}\), are overwritten with \(n_f\) entries of the previous chunk \(a^{\mathrm{prev}}\), counted from the offset \(n_f'\). The second line is the soft part, per slot \(j\): \(v_{\theta,j}\) is what the network wanted there, \(\tilde v_j\) what you integrate instead. The fraction \((a^{\mathrm{prev}}_{n_f'+j} - a^u_j)/(1-u)\) is the constant velocity that would carry the current value to the committed one just as integration finishes at \(u = 1\): distance remaining over flow time remaining. \(W_j\) sets how much of that pull to apply — decaying from 1 to 0 across the anchor region of length \(n_a\), and 0 for the free tail, where the network is left alone.

Two details in that formula bite in practice. The first is the offset \(n_f'\), which is only bookkeeping but is the bookkeeping people get wrong. Slot \(j\) of the new chunk is slot \(n_f'+j\) of the old one, because the new chunk's clock starts \(n_f'\) ticks after the old chunk's; that is why both lines index \(a^{\mathrm{prev}}\) with the offset and never bare \(j\). Both slices are half-open, so each holds exactly \(n_f\) entries, and Section 12.3.4 puts numbers on \(n_f\) and \(n_f'\) together. Code usually applies the offset once up front, shifting the old chunk onto the new chunk's clock, which is what the shift(a_prev, nf_off) line in the Section 12.4 listing does. The second detail is that \(1-u\) goes to zero as integration finishes, so the pull grows without bound at the last step. In exact arithmetic that is harmless, because the distance in the numerator shrinks just as fast. In floating point it is a division by nearly nothing, which is why implementations floor the denominator — the max(1e-3, 1.0 - u) in that same listing is the floor, and it is load-bearing rather than decorative.

Two more observations. First, this is guidance, not retraining: nothing in the weights knows about chunk boundaries, so any flow or diffusion chunk policy supports it out of the box. Second, the correction need not run for the whole integration. Larchenko gates it by a threshold \(u_{ip}\) on the flow time (the tech report writes \(t_{ip}\)), active only once \(u\) passes it, with tuned values around 0.4 to 0.5 — soft inpainting. Early on the sample finds its own shape undragged; the constraint switches on afterward. \(u_{ip}\) is one of the seven knobs.

The alternative in older codebases is temporal ensembling: averaging the overlapping actions of successive chunks instead of constraining generation. It smooths the seam but blurs genuine changes of intent. Black et al. (2025) show that under injected latencies both naive swapping and temporal ensembling degrade, while real-time chunking keeps success rates flat.

12.3.4 Worked example: a latency budget

The knobs interact through a compute budget. Illustrative timings, LeHome's structural parameters.

30 Hz -> tick = 33.3 ms;  n_e = 5 -> re-query every 167 ms
expert passes = K x 2 (CFG) x N = 10 x 2 x 3      = 60
60 x 3 ms + one 55 ms VLM prefix pass             = 235 ms
235 vs 167 available -> 68 late = 2.04 ticks stalled
N 3 -> 2: 40 x 3 + 55                             = 175 ms
n_f  = ceil(235 / 33.3) = 8 frozen, free tail 30 - 8 = 22
n_f' = n_e = 5    (new chunk slot 0 = old chunk slot 5)
generations in flight = ceil(235 / 167)            = 2

Read what that says, one arrangement at a time. Run this synchronously — stop, look, think, move — and you stall the full 235 ms at every boundary, because nothing overlaps: the arm simply waits out the whole forward pass. Pipeline it naively instead, generating chunk \(k{+}1\) while chunk \(k\) runs, and you still come up 68 ms short each time, because 235 ms of work does not fit in a 167 ms window. That is about two ticks per boundary and six boundaries per second, so roughly 12 of every 30 control ticks are stalled — 40% of the robot's time spent waiting on a network. Cutting \(N\) from 3 to 2 nearly closes the gap, and costs you the veto benefit of Section 12.5.

Now be precise about what real-time chunking does and does not fix here, because this is where careful readers get stuck. It does not make the 68 ms disappear. It makes the seam smooth. The throughput deficit is a separate problem with two honest answers: keep two generations in flight at all times, since 235 ms of latency against a 167 ms re-query interval needs depth \(\lceil 235/167 \rceil = 2\); or lengthen \(n_e\) until one generation fits inside one interval. Inpainting is orthogonal to both. What it buys is that when the new chunk lands, the arm does not jerk.

And the freeze is not free either, which the \(n_f = 8\) line makes concrete. Eight slots committed at 33.3 ms each is 267 ms during which the robot will execute what it already decided no matter what it sees — the sliding sleeve of 12.2.1, arriving inside that window, waits. That is exactly the staleness cost a whole section was spent establishing, and it has not been abolished; it has been paid deliberately, in a place where it is smaller than the discontinuity it replaces. The rest is comfortable: with \(n_f' = n_e = 5\), the freeze copies \(a^{\mathrm{prev}}_{5:13}\) into the new chunk's slots 0 through 7, leaving 22 slots generated freely — far more than the 5 you will actually execute before re-querying.

12.4 Classifier-free guidance: asking for more than the data showed

12.4.1 What we want, and why plain conditioning is not enough

Chapter 10 gave you an advantage-conditioned policy: set the condition to \(c_A\), "this was a good execution," and the policy imitates the good part of its own data.

The obvious thing is to just do that: set the token, sample, done. It helps — less than you would hope, and the reason is in the training procedure. Recall the gating from Chapter 10: chunks with negative advantage always get the neutral token, positive chunks are masked stochastically, the probability of going neutral ramping from 0.5 down to 0.1. So a large share of training frames — plausibly most, once the plain behavior-cloning and DAgger data are counted alongside the advantage-labeled frames — carry a neutral condition. Be careful with that claim: the tech report gives the gating rule but not the resulting fraction, so this is the reading that best explains what follows rather than a reported number. Such a network learns to be a good unconditional model first and leans on the advantage token weakly. Switching it on nudges the velocity field; it does not transform it.

What we want is stronger: a policy that acts more like the good episodes than any single good episode did. Here is what makes that possible. The same stochastic masking means one network has learned two velocity fields at once: \(v_\theta(a^u,u,o,\varnothing)\), typical behavior, and \(v_\theta(a^u,u,o,c_A)\), good behavior. The gating is exactly the condition dropout of classifier-free guidance (Ho and Salimans, 2022) — randomly replacing the condition with a null token during training so one model serves as both generators.

12.4.2 The fix: extrapolate along the difference

If you have both fields, their difference is meaningful: \(v_\theta(\cdot, c_A) - v_\theta(\cdot,\varnothing)\) points from "what the policy would do anyway" toward "what it does when told to be good." Rather than taking one step of that difference, take \(g\). At each of the \(K\) integration steps, run the action expert twice and step along the extrapolated field:

\[ \tilde v(a^u,u,o)\;=\;v_\theta(a^u,u,o,\varnothing)\;+\;g\,\bigl[\,v_\theta(a^u,u,o,c_A)\;-\;v_\theta(a^u,u,o,\varnothing)\,\bigr] \]
In plain words
The left side, \(\tilde v\), is the velocity you actually integrate with — the direction the candidate chunk moves this sampling step. \(a^u\) is the partially-formed chunk, \(u\) its flow time, \(o\) the observation. \(v_\theta(\ldots,\varnothing)\) is the output with the condition nulled (average behavior), \(v_\theta(\ldots,c_A)\) the output with it set to "good" (above-average behavior). The bracket is the difference, a small vector pointing from average toward good; \(g\), the guidance scale, says how many copies of it to add. At \(g = 1\) the two \(v_\theta(\ldots,\varnothing)\) terms cancel and you get plain conditional sampling; at \(g = 5\) you move five times as far in the good direction as the conditional model proposed.

Figure 12.2 draws all three vectors at one point: guidance is not a new direction, it is the same one walked further. Why does that help rather than just being wrong? The answer needs one step of Bayes, so let us take it slowly rather than assert it.

Start with what conditioning already means. Bayes says \(p(a \mid o, c_A) \propto p(a \mid o)\,p(\text{good} \mid a, o)\): the probability of chunk \(a\) given that we asked for a good execution is the probability of \(a\) under the policy's ordinary behavior, reweighted by how likely \(a\) is to turn out well. Read the pieces. \(p(a \mid o)\) is the prior, what the policy would do anyway. \(p(\text{good} \mid a, o)\) is a classifier: given this observation and this chunk, how probable is a good outcome? Nobody trained that classifier; it is implied by the two velocity fields the network already learned. Ordinary conditional sampling carries exactly one factor of it.

Guided sampling with scale \(g\) draws instead from a distribution proportional to \(p(a \mid o, c_A)\,p(\text{good} \mid a,o)^{\,g-1}\) — the conditional distribution, tilted by \(g-1\) extra copies of that classifier. Substitute the Bayes expression for the first factor and the classifier terms combine, since \(x^1 x^{g-1} = x^{g}\):

\[ p(a \mid o)\,p(\text{good} \mid a,o)\;\cdot\;p(\text{good} \mid a,o)^{\,g-1} \;=\; p(a \mid o)\,p(\text{good} \mid a,o)^{\,1 + (g-1)} \;=\; p(a \mid o)\,p(\text{good} \mid a,o)^{\,g} \]

So the whole effect of guidance is to sample from the policy's ordinary distribution with an implicit success classifier raised to the power \(g\) — sharpening a success detector you never built. Check the reduction two ways. At \(g = 1\) the first form's exponent is zero, the extra factor becomes 1, and you are back to ordinary conditional sampling; the second form gives \(p(a\mid o)\,p(\text{good}\mid a,o)\), which by Bayes is the same thing. This is the cleanest sense in which a conditioning policy can beat its own average data.

One piece of honesty about that result. It is proved for diffusion models, where the network estimates a score \(\nabla_a \log p\) and the algebra of tilted distributions goes through exactly. Flow matching learns a velocity field, which is related to the score but not identical to it, and the derivation is not redone here or in most papers. Carrying the tilted-distribution story across to flow velocity fields as-is is what everyone does, the \(\pi\)-family included, and it works in practice. Hold it as an inherited justification, not one this chapter established.

12.4.3 The surprising empirical result

How far can you push \(g\)? Image generation typically uses 1.5 to 8, with artifacts at the top of that range, and robotics usually far less. Larchenko searched 0 to 2 — a reasonable range. The bandit of Section 12.6 kept pinning the top arm. He extended the ladder; it kept pinning the top arm. It settled at \(g\) between 7 and 9 by garment type, which he calls "surprisingly high."

Two explanations, both worth internalizing because they tell you when to expect the same thing. First, the conditioning signal is weak by construction: a large share of training frames carry a masked condition, so the conditional–unconditional difference is a small vector needing a large multiplier. Second, the object being generated is forgiving. A natural image has 200,000 dimensions in which a small push off the manifold produces visible garbage; a 30-step chunk of 12-dimensional joint deltas is smooth and heavily constrained, so moderate extrapolation still lands on a feasible motion.

An analogy from photography. Guidance is unsharp masking: to sharpen a photo you subtract a blurred copy and add several multiples of the difference back, \(\text{sharp} = \text{image} + g\,(\text{image} - \text{blur})\). Same formula, same intuition — amplify what distinguishes this thing from its bland version. Where it breaks down: unsharp masking is applied once, to a finished image. Guidance is applied at every one of the \(K\) steps, and each amplified step changes the input to the next, so errors compound. That is why too much guidance gives you an arm saturating its joint limits.

The cost is mild: two action-expert passes per integration step, sharing one VLM prefix cache — the expensive part of the model runs once.

prefix = vlm(o)                              # expensive; computed once
a_ref = shift(a_prev, nf_off)                    # old chunk on the NEW chunk's clock
a = T_z * randn(H, d)                        # T_z scales the only noise drawn
for i in range(K):
    u = i / K
    v_unc = expert(a, u, prefix, cond=NULL)  # advantage token masked
    v_con = expert(a, u, prefix, cond=C_A)   # advantage token = "good"
    v = v_unc + g * (v_con - v_unc)          # g = 1 -> plain conditioning
    if u > u_ip:                             # inpainting switches on late
        v = v + W * (a_ref - a) / max(1e-3, 1.0 - u)   # floor: 1-u -> 0
    a = a + v / K                            # Euler step of size 1/K
    a[:d] = a_ref[:d]                        # freeze the committed prefix

12.5 Best-of-N with the Q-like head

The last thing we want: never commit to a catastrophic chunk. Not "always pick the optimal chunk" — just never take the one that ends the episode.

The obvious fix is to reduce randomness: lower the noise temperature, take more integration steps, hold the seed fixed so a given observation always yields the same chunk.

That first knob is the seventh on the list, and so far this chapter has only named it, so here it is properly. The noise temperature \(T_z\) (the tech report writes \(\tau\); this book keeps \(\tau\) for a trajectory, as in Chapters 1 and 2, so the temperature gets its own letter) is the scale on the initial noise: instead of starting integration from \(a^0 = z\) with \(z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)\), you start from \(a^0 = T_z z\). Nothing else changes — not the weights, not the velocity field, not the number of steps \(K\). Since the finished chunk at \(u = 1\) is a deterministic function of where integration started — integration itself injects no further randomness, as the next page spells out — shrinking the ball you start from shrinks the spread of the chunks you finish with. At \(T_z \lt 1\) all \(N\) candidates are drawn from a narrower region of noise space and land nearer the same mode: more repeatable, less diverse. At \(T_z \gt 1\) they spread out and you see more of the model's alternatives, the good ones and the bad ones both.

Note where LeHome landed: \(T_z\) between 0.7 and 0.9, which is below the 1.0 the model was trained at. That is worth pausing on, because it is a deliberate choice and not a tuning artifact. Training taught the policy a distribution over plausible chunks; deployment sampled deliberately less of it, trading diversity for reliability. Sampling at the temperature you trained at is a convention, not a law.

But turning \(T_z\) down helps a little and misses the point. Catastrophic samples are usually not noise around a good plan; they are a different mode. At a multimodal decision point — which sleeve to grab first — the sampler occasionally commits to a mode that leads nowhere, and a lower temperature draws that mode more crisply rather than not at all.

So filter instead. Chapter 8's auxiliary heads included an action-conditional one: a Q-like head at the tail of the action expert reading the denoised chunk and predicting a success residual — how much this chunk raises or lowers the episode's success probability. That head turns sampling into search. Recall from Chapter 7 that in a flow policy the initial noise \(z\) is the only source of stochasticity: unlike DDPM-style diffusion sampling, no fresh noise is injected at each step, so fixing the observation and the seed makes integration deterministic. That is exactly what makes \(N\) candidates well-defined — \(N\) seeds, \(N\) chunks, no other randomness in the room. So draw \(N\) chunks from different seeds \(z_1,\dots,z_N\), score each, execute the argmax (Figure 12.3) — the robot analog of best-of-N sampling in language models, where a reward model rescores candidates before one is emitted.

The economics are favorable: cost grows linearly in \(N\) but only in the small action expert, since all candidates share the one VLM prefix pass. In LeHome they are scored by the residual averaged over both guidance passes. Returns diminish fast: \(N = 2\) or 3 helped consistently, beyond 3 nothing. And now the finding that should reshape how you think about verifiers. Larchenko reports the head's correlation with final episode outcome was approximately zero — and selection still helped. That is not a contradiction. Best-of-N is not fine-ranking good chunks; it is vetoing the occasional disaster. Telling two plausible folds apart takes a well-calibrated value function; noticing that one candidate drives the gripper into the table does not. A verifier can be useless at ranking and still useful at rejecting. When every candidate scored negative, the client retried with a larger batch.

Now put \(T_z\) and \(N\) side by side, because they pull against each other and the chapter has been building to this. Best-of-N has something to choose between only if the candidates actually differ, and \(T_z\) is the knob that decides how much they differ. Turn \(T_z\) far enough down and your \(N\) chunks are near-copies of one another: you pay \(N\) times the action-expert cost to pick between three renderings of the same motion, and the veto never fires because there is no disaster in the batch to veto. Turn \(T_z\) up and you get genuine alternatives, including bad ones — more for the veto to catch, and more chances it misses one. The tuned pair, \(T_z\) of 0.7 to 0.9 with \(N\) of 2 to 3, sits where a small amount of spread buys a useful veto. Hold on to this pair for Section 12.6: it is the clearest case in the chapter where tuning each knob as if the others did not exist is visibly the wrong model of the problem.

An analogy from your day job. Run a linter over three candidate patches. It cannot say which is most elegant — its correlation with "good code" is near zero — but it reliably catches the one that does not compile. Where it breaks down: a linter is sound, its rules deterministic. The Q-like head is a learned estimate that can be confidently wrong in a systematic direction, and then best-of-N selects for those errors: \(N \gt 1\) becomes worse than \(N = 1\). Validate selection against random choice first.

12.6 Tuning seven knobs with a bandit

12.6.1 Why grid search is dead on arrival

Count them up: execution length \(n_e\), playback stretch, anchor length \(n_a\), inpainting onset \(u_{ip}\), guidance scale \(g\), noise temperature, best-of-N count \(N\). Seven, each tuned per garment type in LeHome, so really twenty-eight.

The obvious approach is a grid search, and it dies immediately. With only four candidate values per knob that is \(4^7 \approx 16{,}000\) configurations per garment type. Each rollout returns one bit, and a bit is a terrible measurement — telling 70% from 75% confidently takes on the order of a thousand trials. Even at a lenient twenty rollouts per configuration you need 320,000 rollouts of about thirty seconds each: 9.6 million seconds, or roughly 2,670 machine-hours. On the four simulator instances a single rollout box runs, that is about 28 days of wall clock — for one garment type, and you have four. Parallel instances bring the wall clock down; they do not change the shape of the problem, and every hour spent on the grid is an hour not spent collecting training data.

But look at what is already happening. Chapter 14's asynchronous flywheel runs rollout workers continuously, hundreds of episodes a day, to feed the training worker — and every one of those episodes has to pick some value for each knob anyway. Tuning does not need its own budget. It needs to piggyback.

12.6.2 Bandits and Thompson sampling from scratch

A multi-armed bandit is the simplest sequential decision problem: several options ("arms"), each with an unknown success probability, chosen one at a time with the outcome observed after each. No state, no delayed consequence — only the tension between playing what looks best and testing what you are unsure about.

Thompson sampling (Thompson, 1933) resolves that tension without a schedule. For each arm keep a Beta posterior, Beta(\(S\), \(F\)): a distribution over that arm's unknown success rate, \(S\) counting successes plus a prior and \(F\) failures plus a prior. Beta(1,1) is flat — "could be anything." Beta(9,3) is a bump around 0.75 with real width; Beta(90,30) a spike at 0.75. Each episode, draw one sample from every arm's posterior, play the arm whose sample is highest, update its counts.

Exploration falls out of the arithmetic. A wide posterior sometimes draws high by luck, so that arm keeps getting tried; a narrow one draws close to its mean. As evidence accumulates the posteriors narrow, lucky draws get rarer, and allocation concentrates on the winner — no epsilon to decay, no schedule to tune, nothing ruled out by one unlucky early failure.

An analogy you have probably lived. This is an A/B test that reallocates traffic as it runs, rather than splitting 50/50 for two weeks and then deciding. Where it breaks down: a web A/B test returns a conversion event in seconds from a stationary system. Your feedback arrives thirty seconds later, is one bit, and the checkpoint is being retrained underneath you — the best \(n_e\) for a clumsy early policy is not the best for a competent late one.

12.6.3 The four adjustments that make it work in practice

Larchenko runs the bandit factorized: one independent bandit per knob, not one over the joint 16,000-cell space. That assumes knob interactions are weak, which is not exactly true — the latency budget above showed \(N\) and \(n_e\) fighting over the same milliseconds, and Section 12.5 showed \(T_z\) and \(N\) pulling in opposite directions on candidate diversity. But it needs evidence on only about 7 knobs \(\times\) 4 candidate values = 28 arms per garment type, instead of \(4^7\) joint cells. (That 28 is a different 28 from the one in 12.6.1, which counted 7 knobs \(\times\) 4 garment types. The collision is an accident of the numbers; these are arms, those were knob instances.) It is the difference between tractable and impossible. Take the assumption knowingly.

Three more adjustments. Centered rewards: reward is success minus the garment type's mean success rate, so an arm is not punished for drawing a hard garment. Unbiased episodes only: replay and hard-mining episodes (Chapter 14) start from restored states with wildly different success rates, so letting them update the bandit would corrupt every posterior. Posterior decay: each checkpoint iteration, shrink posteriors toward the prior so old evidence fades as the policy drifts. Finally the bandit is frozen for submission — you evaluate with fixed knobs, not a still-exploring sampler.

# one Beta bandit per knob; arms = candidate values
S = {arm: 1.0 for arm in arms}    # prior successes: Beta(1,1)
F = {arm: 1.0 for arm in arms}    # prior failures

def choose():
    draws = {arm: np.random.beta(S[arm], F[arm]) for arm in arms}
    return max(draws, key=draws.get)

def update(arm, success):          # after the episode ends
    S[arm] += success
    F[arm] += 1 - success

def decay(factor=0.9):             # once per checkpoint iteration
    for arm in arms:               # forget slowly: the world drifts
        S[arm] = 1 + factor * (S[arm] - 1)
        F[arm] = 1 + factor * (F[arm] - 1)

12.6.4 Worked example: five pulls by hand

Tune \(n_e \in \{3, 5, 10\}\): arms A, B, C, all starting at Beta(1,1), uniform over success probability — we believe nothing. Watch the draws, not the means.

  • Pull 1: draws 0.62, 0.41, 0.77 → play C; episode fails → C becomes Beta(1,2). All three posteriors were identical, so this choice was pure luck of the draw — what "no information" looks like.
  • Pull 2: draws 0.35, 0.88, 0.29 → play B; success → B: Beta(2,1). C drew low partly because its posterior shifted down after that failure.
  • Pull 3: draws 0.71, 0.66, 0.14 → play A; failure → A: Beta(1,2). B just succeeded and still lost: a mean near 0.67 loses to a lucky draw from an untested arm. That is exploration, unscheduled.
  • Pull 4: draws 0.20, 0.93, 0.55 → play B; success → B: Beta(3,1). Now B wins on merit: two successes and no failures put most of its mass above 0.5.
  • Pull 5: draws 0.44, 0.72, 0.61 → play B; failure → B: Beta(3,2). One failure does not undo two successes; it widens B's posterior downward, raising how often A and C win future draws.

After five pulls the posterior means are 0.33 (A), 0.60 (B), 0.33 (C) — that is \(S/(S+F)\): \(1/3\), \(3/5\), \(1/3\). But the next pull is not automatically B, and it is worth seeing exactly why rather than taking it on faith. Arm A's posterior is Beta(1,2), whose density is \(2(1-x)\); arm B's is Beta(3,2), whose density is \(12x^2(1-x)\). The chance A's draw beats B's is one posterior integrated against the other:

\[ P(a \gt b) \;=\; \int_0^1 12b^2(1-b)\left[\int_b^1 2(1-x)\,dx\right]db \;=\; \int_0^1 12b^2(1-b)(1-b)^2\,db \;=\; 12\int_0^1 b^2(1-b)^3\,db \;=\; \frac{12}{60} \;=\; \frac{1}{5} \]

Take that one bracket at a time. The inner integral is the probability that A's draw lands above some particular value \(b\), and for Beta(1,2) it works out to \((1-b)^2\). The outer integral averages that over every value \(b\) that B might draw, weighted by B's own density. The last step uses \(\int_0^1 b^2(1-b)^3 db = 1/60\), a standard Beta integral. Arm C is in exactly A's state, so it too wins one draw in five. The chance that either beats B is about one in three — not two-fifths, because A and C sometimes win the same round, and the same double integral with both untested arms gives 0.33. So A and C keep being tested while B accumulates evidence. That explore–exploit balance, driven entirely by posterior width, is why five noisy rollouts already produce a sensible allocation while a grid search would still be on its first cell.

Pitfalls
(1) A guidance scale pushed too high walks off the action manifold: confident nonsense, jerky saturated motions. Watch the arm as \(g\) grows, not just the success rate. (2) Best-of-N with a miscalibrated Q-like head amplifies its errors: if the head systematically prefers a wrong mode, \(N \gt 1\) is worse than \(N = 1\). Validate against random choice. (3) Bandit feedback is delayed by a whole episode and confounded with checkpoint updates: decay the posteriors, and never update from replay or hard-mining episodes, whose success rates are not comparable.
In the LeHome solution
Seven per-garment-type knobs — execution length, playback stretch, anchor length, inpainting onset, guidance scale, noise temperature, best-of-N — tuned by a factorized Thompson bandit rewarded by success minus the garment's mean success rate. Only unbiased episodes update it, posteriors decay each iteration, and it is frozen for submission. Final values: \(n_e\) 3–5 of 30, \(g\) 7–9, \(N\) 2–3, \(T_z\) 0.7–0.9, \(u_{ip}\) 0.4–0.5. Read \(T_z\) below 1 as sampling deliberately narrower than training implied. The high guidance scale surfaced only because the bandit kept pinning the top arm as the ladder was extended; the report gives no per-knob ablations, so treat individual contributions as unmeasured.
Checkpoint
  • Explain why executing a whole chunk is open-loop control in disguise, and state both sides of the \(n_e\) trade-off with a concrete re-planning rate.
  • Describe how naive asynchronous chunk swapping fails, why delta actions make it worse, what real-time chunking freezes, blends and leaves free, and what \((a^{\mathrm{prev}} - a^u)/(1-u)\), \(W_j\) and \(u_{ip}\) mean in the correction.
  • Write the guidance formula, name every symbol, verify by hand that \(g = 1\) reduces to plain conditional sampling, and give both reasons \(g = 7\) to 9 was viable here when image models use far less.
  • Explain how a verifier with near-zero outcome correlation still improves success, when best-of-N makes a policy worse, and why the noise temperature \(T_z\) and the candidate count \(N\) cannot honestly be tuned as independent knobs.
  • Set up a Thompson bandit for one knob, simulate a few pulls by hand, justify factorization and posterior decay, and build a per-query latency budget from control rate, \(K\), \(N\) and guidance.

Where to go deeper. Real-time chunking is Black et al. (2025) — short and unusually readable, and worth reading before you implement any asynchronous inference. Classifier-free guidance is Ho and Salimans (2022), written for images but applied verbatim to flow-matching velocity fields. The seven-knob inventory, the surprisingly high guidance scales, and the factorized bandit are Section 7 of Larchenko (2026). For Thompson sampling beyond the Beta–Bernoulli case, the tutorial by Russo et al. (2018) is standard.

Chapter 13 — Imitation and the human in the loop

Every chapter so far has assumed a policy already exists and your job is to improve it — with advantage weights in Chapter 4, with more expressive action distributions in Chapters 6 and 7, with advantage conditioning in Chapter 10, with better rewards in Chapter 11. None of that answers the first question: where does the initial policy come from, and what do you do when it is not good enough?

In practice the answer is a human. Someone teleoperates the robot until there is data to train on, and then someone sits beside the robot while it runs and takes over when it is about to do something stupid. That second activity is the cheapest and highest-leverage resource in robot learning, and it is what this chapter is about.

You already run a pipeline built on exactly this idea: an SO-101 arm, an actor process and a learner process, an Xbox pad in your hands, and a working run in which you were intervening 98% of the time. By the end of this chapter you should understand what each piece is doing, why the intervention rate is the number to watch, and why 98% on an early session is the expected starting point rather than a sign of failure.

Words you will hear

Covariate shift — the training inputs and the deployment inputs come from different distributions; in imitation, the demonstrator's states versus the policy's own states. No-regret — a property of an online learning algorithm: as rounds accumulate, its average performance approaches that of the best fixed choice in hindsight; vanilla DAgger inherits it, the human-gated variants of Section 13.3 do not, and they trade it for a labeling cost a person can actually pay. Gate — the switch that decides who is currently commanding the robot, the policy or the human. Intervention — one contiguous segment of human control, from takeover to release. Replay ratio (or update-to-data ratio, UTD) — how many gradient steps the learner takes per new environment transition. Symmetric sampling — forcing every training batch to be half human-sourced data and half fresh online data.

13.1 Behavior cloning and compounding error

13.1.1 What we want, and the obvious thing to try

What we want is a policy that performs the task, and the cheapest route is to record a human performing it and fit a network to the recording. Chapter 4 called this behavior cloning (BC): supervised learning on demonstrated observation–action pairs, identical to AWR's weighted regression with every weight set to one, with no rewards, no rollouts and no credit assignment. Every VLA in Chapter 8 is behavior cloning at scale.

So the obvious thing to try is: collect a hundred demonstrations, train until validation loss stops falling, press run. For short tasks this works better than it has any right to. Then it falls apart, in a way that catches everyone the first time.

13.1.2 How it fails, step by step

Supervised learning gives you one guarantee only: low error on the distribution the training data came from — the states the demonstrator \(\pi_\beta\) visited. Call that set the demo tube, and watch what happens at deployment one step at a time.

At step 0 the robot starts inside the tube, because you reset it the way you always did. The policy predicts an action close to the human's but not identical — a network trained to a finite loss is never exactly right. Say the gripper ends up one millimeter left of where the human's would have been.

At step 1 the robot is therefore slightly off the tube's centerline. It is still inside the tube, so the policy is still reasonably accurate, but a little less accurate than at the center, because this state is a little less represented in the training data. Its next error is a bit larger — say 1.8 millimeters. At step 2 the error is about 3 millimeters, and by now the accumulated offset has carried the gripper out near the tube's edge.

Notice how undramatic that is. Nothing alarming happens on any single step, which is exactly why this failure is hard to catch by watching one frame at a time. The compounding is slow at first, and only becomes visible once the accumulated offset has walked the robot out of the region your demonstrations cover.

At step 3 the robot is outside the tube entirely, and the situation is now qualitatively different. The network has never seen anything like this observation, so its output is not "slightly wrong", it is arbitrary. No gradient anywhere in training ever told it what to do here.

The critical property is that this loop feeds itself. Each error moves the robot to a state where the policy is worse, and a worse policy produces a larger error, which moves the robot somewhere worse still. It is not a nuisance that averages out; it is positive feedback. Figure 13.1 is the picture to keep in your head.

Two different things are going on here, and it is worth separating them before the next section, because they blur together easily. What you just walked through is a mechanism: why one mistake tends to lead to another, larger mistake. The \(T^2\) in the bound below comes from something simpler and more countable — how many mistakes you expect over an episode, multiplied by how long each one keeps hurting. The walkthrough is the intuition; the counting argument is the proof. So do not read the millimeter numbers as a growth law: a policy whose error truly multiplied by four every step would be off the table inside two seconds, and cloning would never work at all.

13.1.3 Why the damage is quadratic

There is a classic result that makes this precise, and it comes in two halves with two different sources: the quadratic side is Ross and Bagnell (2010), and the linear side is the DAgger analysis of Ross et al. (2011), which Section 13.2 comes to. Let \(\epsilon\) be the per-step mistake rate of the learned policy measured on the demonstrator's distribution — the supervised error rate, which in the imitation literature is universally written \(\epsilon\); this is not the PPO clip parameter of Chapter 3, and the collision of symbols is unfortunate but standard. Let \(T\) be the episode length in steps, and let \(J\) be the expected cost of running a policy for one episode. Then:

\[ J\big(\pi_\theta^{\text{BC}}\big) \;\le\; J(\pi_\beta) + \mathcal{O}\!\left(\epsilon T^{2}\right), \qquad J\big(\pi_\theta^{\text{DAgger}}\big) \;\le\; J(\pi_\beta) + \mathcal{O}\!\left(\epsilon T\right). \]
In plain words

\(J\) is the expected cost of one episode — how much worse than perfect the run is, summed over its steps. \(J(\pi_\beta)\) is the cost of the human demonstrator: the standard you are trying to match. \(\pi_\theta^{\text{BC}}\) is the policy you get from plain behavior cloning, \(\pi_\theta^{\text{DAgger}}\) the one you get from the method in Section 13.2. \(\epsilon\) is how often the learned policy picks a bad action on the demonstrator's states, as a fraction between 0 and 1. \(T\) is the number of steps in an episode. \(\mathcal{O}(\cdot)\) means "grows like, up to a constant factor". So the whole statement reads: cloning can be worse than the human by an amount that grows with the square of the episode length, while the corrected method pays only in proportion to the episode length. Doubling how long the task takes quadruples one penalty and merely doubles the other.

Where does the square come from? Two factors of \(T\) multiply. The first is how many mistakes you expect: at rate \(\epsilon\) over \(T\) steps, roughly \(\epsilon T\) of them. The second is what each mistake costs: a mistake at step \(t\) can push you off-distribution, and once off-distribution you may stay there for all \(T - t\) remaining steps, so one mistake is charged for up to \(T\) bad steps rather than one. Multiply and you get \(\epsilon T^2\). DAgger removes the second factor by measuring \(\epsilon\) on the policy's own states, where a mistake is just one bad step in a place the policy was trained — it does not open a trapdoor.

13.1.4 A small worked example: how good would BC have to be?

Put your own numbers on it. Your SO-101 runs autonomously at 30 Hz (Chapter 4's convention: 20 Hz when you are teleoperating through the leader arm, 30 Hz when the policy drives), so a 20-second task is \(T = 600\) steps.
